title: Consultation Chats
description: Thirty scripts for talking to patients about what a consultation is really like, and why a good one feels like a chat.

items.hook: Wondering what actually happens in a first consultation? Here it is, minute by minute
items.script:
Let me walk you through it. You arrive, and we start with a cup of tea and a chat. I ask what brought you in, what you have been thinking about, and what you would like to feel when you look in the mirror.

Then I go through your medical history, because your safety shapes every decision I make. I look at your face in natural light, and we talk through your options at your pace. If a treatment suits you, I explain what it involves, how it feels and what the aftercare looks like.

You leave with a plan and plenty of time to think. Many people book nothing on the day, and that is a perfectly good outcome.

Along the way I take notes, and at the end I read them back so you can check I heard you properly. You also get my contact details and a written summary to take home. Most people tell me they expected a sales conversation and found a thoughtful chat instead, and that surprise is my favourite part of the job.

If you have been curious for a while, send me a message and we can find a time that suits you. What is the one question you would bring along?

items.hook: Three questions worth bringing to every aesthetic consultation
items.script:
Here are the three I hope you will bring along. First, what is your training, and who supervises your practice? A good practitioner answers that with a smile.

Second, what happens if I am unhappy afterwards? A clear aftercare plan tells you a lot about the clinic.

Third, what would you suggest I leave alone? That one is my favourite. It shows whether the person across the table is advising you or selling to you.

Write these in your phone before you arrive. I love a patient with a notes page full of questions, because it means we will have a proper conversation.

There is a bonus fourth question I love: how will you know when something has gone well? It makes us agree on the finish line before we begin. Patients who ask it tend to feel much calmer, because they know exactly what we are both aiming for and how we will check in on the way.

Save this for your next appointment. Which question would you add to the list?

items.hook: You can say stop at any point in your appointment, and I will listen
items.script:
I say this out loud at the start of every treatment. If you want a pause, a sip of water or a full stop, you only have to say so.

Nerves are very common, and they deserve respect. I check in as I go, and I would much rather stop and reset than carry on with a patient who feels uneasy.

Your comfort and consent run through the whole appointment, from the first chat to the last goodbye. You hold the controls from start to finish.

I also ask you to give me a small signal, like lifting a finger, so you never need to find the words while you are mid treatment. Patients tell me this simple agreement lets them relax their shoulders, because the exit door is always open. It takes ten seconds to set up and it changes the whole mood of the room.

If you have been putting off a consultation because you worry about feeling stuck in the chair, message me. I will talk you through exactly how we work. What would help you feel most at ease?

items.hook: The very first thing I ask every new patient
items.script:
Before anything else, I ask, what would you like to feel when you look in the mirror?

The answers surprise me every time. Rested. More like myself. Ready for a big birthday. Less cross when the camera comes out on a Zoom call.

Notice that nobody says, give me a stranger's face. People want to feel like themselves on a good day, and that gives me a lovely direction to work in.

It also tells me when a treatment will suit you and when something simpler might help, like a skincare routine or a longer break from a worry.

Sometimes the answer is a feeling, and sometimes it is a date, like a wedding or a reunion. Either helps. A feeling points me towards balance and a date points me towards timing, and between the two we can build a plan that suits your life.

If you have an answer already, I would love to hear it. What would yours be?

items.hook: Nervous about your first aesthetic appointment? Here is how I look after you
items.script:
I have a little routine for first timers. We take our time with a proper chat first, before I pick up anything.

I explain each step before it happens, in plain English, so you always know what comes next. I keep my voice calm, I offer water, and I invite you to tell me when you would like a pause.

Plenty of my patients tell me afterwards that the build up was worse than the appointment. That is common, and we can make the build up gentler too, with a call or a message beforehand.

I also suggest a quick call or a visit to see the clinic before your appointment. Walking through the door once makes the second time feel familiar. Some patients bring a book or a favourite playlist, and a few simply bring a friend to sit in the waiting area. Whatever helps, I am happy to make room for it.

If butterflies are the only thing standing between you and a consultation, send me a message. What would make you feel most welcome?

items.hook: How I read a face before I suggest anything at all
items.script:
I start by watching you talk. Faces move, and the way yours smiles, frowns and tires tells me far more than a still photograph.

Then I look at your skin, your bone structure, the way light falls across your features and where you tend to hold tension. I ask you to point out what you notice, because you know your own face better than I do.

Only after that do I suggest anything, and sometimes the suggestion is to wait, or to start with the smallest step.

I pay attention to symmetry too, because every face has natural differences between left and right. I will point them out gently so nothing surprises you later. Knowing your own face well helps you judge results fairly, and it helps me choose a plan that respects the way your features already balance.

This careful look is what keeps results balanced and recognisably you. Would you like to see how it works in person? Message me and we will book a consultation.

items.hook: Why I ask so many questions about your health history
items.script:
It can feel like a lot of paperwork, and I promise it has a purpose. Your medical history, medications, allergies and past treatments all shape what is safe for you.

Some details change my advice completely. A medication, a recent illness, a pregnancy, an upcoming holiday. If something comes up, I would much rather know in the consultation than find out later.

Everything you share stays confidential and goes into your record, which I keep safely.

Think of it as a safety net with lots of small holes covered. A pharmacy list, a recent course of antibiotics or a new supplement can all affect timing. When you share them, I can adjust the plan or suggest a different date, and you go home safer. Nothing you tell me shocks me, and I treat every detail with respect.

So when I ask the long list of questions, picture me being thorough because I care about you getting home well. Is there anything you wish clinics asked you more about?

items.hook: Why I sometimes suggest waiting before any treatment
items.script:
If a patient sits across from me unsure, I tell them to go home and think. I mean it kindly, and I mean it every time.

A decision that feels right tomorrow is worth much more than a yes squeezed out today. Some people come back within a week, some within a year, and a few discover they were happy as they were.

I love all three outcomes. The best patient relationships begin with a sense of calm.

Sometimes, when we meet again, the idea has changed shape entirely. A patient may realise she wanted something smaller, or something else, or nothing at all. That feels like a win to me, because the decision came from her and from a calm mind. Leaving a gap protects your choices and your budget.

You are welcome to bring your questions, take your notes and leave with nothing booked. When would you like to start the conversation?

items.hook: The two minutes at the start of every appointment when I just listen
items.script:
After you sit down, I stay quiet. For two minutes, you talk and I listen.

It is my favourite part of the day. People tell me what they truly want, often in a sentence they have not said to anyone else. A wedding, a divorce, a new job, a moment they caught themselves in the mirror and felt a stranger looked back.

Those two minutes shape everything after them. They keep me focused on you, and they give you space to be heard before anyone starts planning.

Afterwards, I summarise what I heard in a sentence or two, so you know I took it in. People often nod and say, yes, that is it exactly. If I have it slightly wrong, you can correct me, and we adjust the plan before anything happens. It sets the tone for honest conversation.

Have you ever had a consultation where you felt properly listened to? What made it feel that way?

items.hook: Bring the one photo that sums up how you want to feel
items.script:
Scroll through your camera roll before your consultation. Find a picture of yourself where you felt great. Maybe it is a holiday photo, a wedding, an ordinary Tuesday where the light was kind.

Show me that picture. It tells me so much more than a list of concerns. I can see your natural expression, what you like about yourself and the version of you that feels most like you.

Please skip the celebrity photos. They send us in the wrong direction, because your face deserves a plan of its own.

You might also bring a photo of something that bothers you, like an angle caught in a car window. Showing me is easier than describing it. We can look at it together and talk through what you see. Pictures help us find the same words for the same worry, which makes the whole plan clearer.

Which photo would you pick?

items.hook: How I decide what to suggest and what to leave alone
items.script:
I use a simple order. Safety comes first, then your goals, then what suits your face, and then what suits your budget and your calendar.

If a treatment would not suit you, I say so. If a smaller step would do the job, I suggest that first. If something else would help more, like a skincare change or a quiet look at sleep and stress, I mention it.

My aim is for you to leave feeling clear. If I have recommended three things, you should know why for each of them.

I explain the reasons behind each suggestion in everyday language, and I list the options from gentlest to most involved. You can choose the first step and leave the rest for later. If you ever feel I have said too much, tell me, and I will simplify it. Clarity matters more to me than a long list.

Would you like help working out where to begin? Send me a message and we will find a time for a consultation.

items.hook: What a good consultation feels like from the patient's chair
items.script:
A good consultation feels like talking to a knowledgeable friend. You sit comfortably. Nobody rushes you. The person across from you asks about your life as well as your face.

You hear honest answers, including the ones that mean waiting or skipping a treatment. You see written information you can take home. You can ask the same question twice without anyone sighing.

You leave knowing what happens next, and you feel free to say no.

Afterwards you should feel lighter, even if you decided to wait. You should know your next step, who to contact and what to think about at home. If you leave feeling confused or pressured, something went wrong in the room. A consultation should leave you with more confidence than you arrived with.

If you have had a consultation that felt different, you deserve better. What would your ideal consultation look like?

items.hook: The questions I love being asked in clinic
items.script:
I adore a patient who asks, what happens if I do not like it? Or, who do I call at nine at night if something worries me?

I also love, how many treatments have you done like this one? And, would you have this yourself?

These questions help me do my job better. They tell me you care about your safety, and they push me to explain things clearly.

Another favourite: what would you do in my position? It invites a real answer, and it often leads to the most useful part of the chat. I also like, how will you check my work? Because I enjoy explaining my reviews. Curious patients help me stay sharp and honest.

If you are heading to a consultation soon, take your questions and read them out loud. A good practitioner is delighted to answer. Which one would you ask first?

items.hook: What to wear, eat and bring to your first appointment
items.script:
Wear something comfortable, and arrive with a clean face if you can. If you wear make up, no worries at all, we can take it off.

Eat something beforehand, and bring a bottle of water. Bring a list of your medications, any allergies and your questions. A friend is welcome if that makes you feel steadier.

Leave a little time afterwards so you are not rushing to a meeting with your coat half on.

Wear a top that is easy to move around in, and avoid heavy collars if we are looking at your neck. Leave jewellery at home if you can. If you have long hair, bring a clip. Little things make the visit smoother, and I keep spare hair bands in the room just in case.

That is the whole checklist. Anything you would like to add before your first visit? Tell me in the comments.

items.hook: Consent forms explained in plain English
items.script:
A consent form is a written record of a conversation we have already had. It lists what the treatment is, what it involves, the possible side effects and what to do if you have concerns.

I go through every line with you, and you can take it home before you decide. You can ask me to explain a word, and you can ask me to repeat it.

Signing means you understand what we have discussed and that you agree to go ahead. You can change your mind afterwards too.

There is usually a section on risks, and I read it aloud so you hear the words said calmly. We discuss each risk, how likely it is and what we would do. I also explain the cooling off time I offer, and I make sure you have a copy to read at home. It is your document, so take your time with it.

If a clinic ever hands you a form and a pen with no explanation, that deserves a question. Have you ever signed something without reading it?

items.hook: Why I take photographs at your appointment and where they go
items.script:
I take photos at the start so we have an honest record of how things looked on day one. They help me plan your treatment and track how things change over time.

They live in your confidential patient record, stored securely. I only share them with your written permission, and you can say no to any use beyond your own record.

I keep the lighting, angle and expression the same each time, so the comparison is fair.

Photos also help me spot small changes that are easy to forget, like how a brow sat or how a shadow fell. When you see your comparison at a review, it can be a lovely moment, since memory can be unreliable. I mean it when I say you can ask me to delete them if you change your mind.

If a clinic takes your photo and cannot tell you what happens to it, ask. What would you want to know about your records?

items.hook: How long a consultation takes and what fills the time
items.script:
Plan for about thirty to forty five minutes. Most of that is conversation.

We spend ten minutes on your story and goals, ten on health history and consent, and ten or fifteen looking at your face and discussing options. The rest is for questions and a plan.

If you would like to treat on the same day, I may offer that. When you are unsure, I suggest booking separately so you have a night to sleep on it.

Treatments themselves vary a lot in length, and I tell you before you book. If you have a tight schedule, say so, and we will plan around it. Booking a consultation first means your treatment day can feel unhurried, with all the questions already answered and the paperwork done.

Does that match what you imagined? Tell me in the comments what you thought a consultation involved.

items.hook: Why I offer you thinking time before any treatment
items.script:
After your consultation, I send you home with notes and a gentle suggestion to take your time. A day, a week, a month. Whatever feels right.

Thinking time gives you a chance to talk it over with someone you trust, read the aftercare, and notice whether the idea still excites you.

It also protects you from deciding in the glow of a lovely conversation. I want you to book because you are sure.

I find thinking time works best with a few simple tasks. Reread your notes, talk to a friend, check my reviews and see how you feel after a good night's sleep. If a question pops up, send it to me. I enjoy those messages, and I reply as soon as I can with a calm, clear answer.

Does thinking time feel like a relief or a frustration? I would love to hear which.

items.hook: What I really mean when I say natural looking
items.script:
To me it means that friends tell you that you look well and rested, and nobody can say exactly why.

It means your expressions still move, your features still balance and your face still looks like yours. It also means going gently, with small steps and a review before more.

Different patients picture different things when they hear the phrase, so I always ask you to show me what natural means to you.

I might show you photos of expressions that feel balanced, and ask you to point to the ones that suit you best. We talk about eyebrows, smiles and the way your face moves. Natural looking is a shared language, so I like us to practise it together before any plan is made.

What does it mean in your head? Tell me, and we will start there.

items.hook: Should you bring a friend to your consultation? Here is my take
items.script:
I love it when patients bring someone. A friend or a sister can ask the questions you forget, and they remember what we discussed.

Choose a person who supports you and respects your decision. Their job is to listen and help you think, and the decision belongs to you.

I will always make time to speak with you privately for part of the consultation, because some questions are easier on your own.

If your friend is nervous too, bring a second friend! I joke, but a lovely companion can make the whole visit feel lighter. Afterwards, patients often say the best part was having someone who understood why they came. I never mind an audience that cheers you on quietly.

Who would you bring? Tell me about them in the comments.

items.hook: A first appointment jitters checklist you can read in your car
items.script:
Sit in your car for two minutes and run through this. Breathe in for four and out for six, a few times. Remind yourself that you can ask any question, and that you can say stop whenever you like.

Check you have your medication list, your questions and your photo ID if the clinic asked for it. Drink some water. Loosen your shoulders, because most of us arrive with them up by our ears.

Walk in, say hello, and tell the first person you meet that you are a little nervous. Every clinic worth its salt will make a fuss of you.

Another trick: pick a small reward for afterwards, like a coffee, a walk or a favourite show. It turns a nervous morning into a gentle treat. I have seen patients arrive tense and leave smiling about their plans for the afternoon. A kind ending shapes how you remember the whole experience.

You have already done the hardest bit by booking. What helps calm you before something new?

items.hook: What happens if you change your mind halfway through a treatment day
items.script:
Then we stop, and that is the end of the matter. I mean it every single time.

Changing your mind is a normal and healthy part of making a decision about your face. Sometimes the room, the quiet or the reality of it all makes a person realise they need more time. I would rather you tell me than push on to be polite.

We talk it through, make you a cup of tea, and rebook if you would like to. Nothing awkward happens, and nothing is wasted.

You will never owe me an explanation for stopping, and I will never add a charge for the time we spent talking. I simply note what we covered in your record, and I leave the door open for another day. Patients often return months later, more certain, and I welcome them like old friends.

A good clinic welcomes honesty in the treatment room. Has anyone ever made you feel rushed? Tell me, I would love to know how it felt.

items.hook: Why I ask about your sleep, stress and daily routine
items.script:
Your face reflects your life. Sleep, stress, sun, diet, hydration and the products you use all show up on your skin and in your expression.

When I ask about your week, I am looking for clues. A new job, a baby, a run of late nights or a holiday in the sun can explain a concern that you assumed needed a treatment.

Sometimes the best advice is a small change at home, and I would rather tell you that than book you in. When a treatment does suit you, knowing your routine helps me plan around it.

It also helps me suggest a realistic plan. If you work nights, travel often or spend a lot of time outdoors, that changes my advice. A treatment that fits your life tends to feel easier and give you more joy. Planning around your routine shows you that I listen.

What does a normal week look like for you? Tell me what you would change.

items.hook: What happens at your follow up appointment and why it matters
items.script:
Around two weeks after a treatment, I invite patients back for a review. It gives me the chance to see how things have settled and to check how you feel.

We look at your results together in the same light and the same position as day one. I ask about your experience, the aftercare and anything unexpected. If a small adjustment is helpful, we discuss it then.

The review also gives you a named person to ask questions. Many patients tell me it was the part that made them feel safe.

At the review I also check your skincare and answer any questions that popped up since we last spoke. You can bring photographs you took at home, and we compare them with mine. If something deserves a closer look, we book another visit. Nothing is left hanging, and you always know the next step.

Does a clinic you use offer reviews? Tell me what yours does.

items.hook: The honest things I will tell you in a consultation
items.script:
I will tell you what a treatment can do and what it cannot. I will tell you how it might feel, how long it tends to last and what a realistic outcome looks like for your face.

I will tell you about possible side effects, and I will tell you when I think a different route would suit you better.

I would much rather lose a booking than send you home with the wrong expectations.

I will also tell you how treatments behave over time, so you know what to expect in a few months as well as a few days. Some effects soften gradually, and some are quick to appear. Knowing the full arc helps you plan and keeps surprises to a minimum.

Being honest takes a bit more time and it builds trust that lasts for years. What do you most want a practitioner to be honest about?

items.hook: How I choose the products and brands I use in my clinic
items.script:
I choose carefully. I look at safety records, the reputation of the manufacturer, the evidence behind a product and how it behaves in real faces.

I keep my supplier details, batch numbers and expiry dates, and I record them in your notes. If you ever need to know exactly what was used, I can tell you.

I stay with the options I trust, even when something new is being talked about on social media.

I also keep up with safety notices and ask suppliers hard questions. If a product changes, I explain why I switched. Patients are welcome to see the packaging and ask me anything about it. Open conversations about products build trust, and I enjoy them.

Do you check what a clinic uses on you? A good practitioner will always tell you. What would you like to ask?

items.hook: Why I ask you to look in the mirror with me
items.script:
Mirrors help us have a proper conversation. I hand you one and ask you to show me what you notice.

You might point to something I had not spotted, and I might see that the thing you love is the thing you want to keep. Sometimes you say, I never noticed that before, and we both laugh.

Looking together keeps us on the same page, and it stops me guessing. You lead and I follow, with my training to guide us both.

It is also a gentle way to check that we are aiming at the same feature. Sometimes patients point to a spot I would not have picked, and it reveals what really bothers them. Other times they notice something lovely about themselves for the first time. Either way, the mirror turns our chat into teamwork.

When did you last look in the mirror and simply smile? Tell me about it.

items.hook: Booking your consultation in three simple steps
items.script:
Step one: choose a time that suits your diary. Pick a day when you are not rushing, because calm helps.

Step two: fill in the short health form we send you, so we can use your time together well.

Step three: write down your questions, and bring them along. That is the whole process.

You pay for a consultation in some clinics, and in others it is free. Ask when you book, so there are no surprises. And you can always turn up, listen and go home with nothing booked.

If you cannot find a suitable time, just ask. I keep a few early and late slots for people who work around school runs or shifts. You can also message me with questions before booking, and I will reply as soon as I can. Making it simple matters to me.

What would stop you booking a consultation? Tell me, and I will try to help.

items.hook: The question about my training that I wish more patients asked
items.script:
Ask me about it. I will happily tell you.

I trained as a healthcare professional first, then completed specialist courses in aesthetic treatments, and I keep learning every year with practical sessions and supervised cases. I carry insurance, I follow current guidance, and I work with a medical prescriber where the law requires one.

I enjoy sharing my certificates and my route, because I am proud of the work it took.

I also enjoy talking about the people who taught me. Good mentors shape how we work, and I share what I learnt from them. You are welcome to ask how I stay up to date, and I will happily show you my training records and the courses I plan to take next.

Any practitioner who shrugs off this question deserves another one. What would you ask about my training?

items.hook: Your consultation, start to finish, in sixty seconds
items.script:
You arrive and we say hello over a cup of tea. I ask about you, what you would like and how you feel about your face.

Then we cover your health history, your medication and any allergies. I take photos in natural light. We look in the mirror together, and I explain what I notice and what might suit you.

I describe your options, the costs, the aftercare and the risks, and you ask anything you like. We agree a plan, or we agree you will think about it.

Every step is yours to pause, repeat or skip. If you want more time on any part, say so. The aim is for you to leave knowing what you want to do, and what you would like to wait on. A consultation works best when you feel in charge of the pace.

You leave with written notes and no pressure. Does that match what you pictured?

title: Myths Answered
description: Thirty scripts that gently answer the things patients whisper to their friends.

items.hook: "Everyone will know I've had something done." Let me answer that gently
items.script:
It is one of the worries I hear most, and it comes from a good place. People remember the overdone faces they have seen and fear the same for themselves.

Here is what I do instead. I start small and review before adding anything. I look at balance, so one feature never shouts louder than the rest. I keep your expressions moving and I check how you look when you laugh, talk and frown.

The aim is for friends to say you look well, rested or happy, and to wonder what changed.

I also invite you to bring a friend or a photo, so we can talk about what natural means to you. Every patient has a different picture in mind, and mine only helps if it matches yours. A slow, stepwise approach lets you grow into any change and tell me when it feels right.

Everyone's face is different, so I never promise a particular outcome. I do promise a careful plan. Does that worry sound familiar? Tell me about yours.

items.hook: Myth: you have to keep going once you start. Here is the truth
items.script:
You can stop whenever you like. Nothing locks you in.

Treatments last for a period of time and then gradually fade, and your face returns to where it would have been. Some patients choose to repeat. Others take a break, change their mind or move on to something different.

A good practitioner reviews with you every time and checks you still want to continue. I like knowing that every visit is a choice you make freshly.

I like to say that you hold the steering wheel. Some patients enjoy a regular schedule because it fits their routine, and some prefer a long gap. Neither choice is better. What matters is that you feel free to decide each time, with accurate information and without pressure from anyone.

Have you ever worried about getting stuck on a treadmill? Tell me what you have heard, and I will answer honestly.

items.hook: Does it hurt? An honest answer from someone who does this daily
items.script:
It depends on the treatment, the area and the person. Most patients describe a pinch, a pressure or a quick sting, and some barely notice anything.

I can reduce discomfort in several ways. I can use numbing cream or ice, work slowly, choose fine needles and talk to you throughout. If you have a low pain threshold, tell me, and we adapt.

A promise of feeling nothing would be a fib, so my promise is to look after you carefully, to be straight about what you might feel and to stop whenever you ask.

For some people, a good chat and a deep breath make the biggest difference. I time my movements to your breathing, I tell you before each step and I never surprise you. A pause costs nothing, and I would much prefer you tell me you need one than grit your teeth through it.

What worries you most about discomfort? Let me know, and we will plan around it.

items.hook: "I'm too young to start." The conversation I have with twenty somethings
items.script:
Age is only one piece of the picture. I would much rather talk about your goals, your skin and your lifestyle.

Often the best advice for someone in their twenties is sun protection, a gentle skincare routine and patience. Prevention is largely about everyday habits, and those cost far less than a clinic visit.

Some younger patients do have a specific concern, and we discuss whether a treatment suits them. I take care to ask what is motivating the request, because it matters.

I also ask what you enjoy about your face right now, because a young face has plenty to celebrate. Sometimes a quick chat reassures a patient so much that she leaves with no booking and a lighter heart. That feels like a success to me, and I am always glad to see her again whenever she wishes.

If you are curious, come for a chat. We can talk about skin, habits and what suits you now. How old were you when you first thought about it?

items.hook: "I'm too old to start." Here is what I tell my over fifties
items.script:
There is no clock on caring for yourself. Many of my loveliest patients came to me in their fifties, sixties and beyond.

Skin changes through the decades, and a thoughtful plan respects that. We talk about what has changed, what bothers you and what you want to keep. Often a well chosen, gentle approach feels better than a bigger intervention.

I also make sure your health history is up to date, as it matters more with time.

Over time I have noticed that my patients in their fifties and beyond ask the most thoughtful questions. They know their own minds and they appreciate straight answers. I enjoy those conversations hugely, and I find that a measured, respectful plan tends to bring lovely feedback from friends and family.

You are welcome here at any age, and the conversation always begins with listening. What would you like to feel more like?

items.hook: "Will I look frozen?" What I do to keep your expression alive
items.script:
This is the fear I hear most from my patients. It deserves a straight answer.

A frozen look usually comes from using too much in the wrong places. I aim for a light touch, I plan around how your face moves, and I review you at two weeks to see how things settled.

Your smile, your frown and your raised eyebrow are part of how people know you. I want you to keep them.

I take photographs of your expressions during the consultation, so we both see how your face moves before any plan begins. It helps me avoid heavy changes in the places that matter most for your character. You are very welcome to tell me which expressions you adore, and I will make a note of them.

Every face behaves differently, so I cannot make promises, and I can promise to talk through every step. Do you have a feature you want to keep moving? Tell me which.

items.hook: Myth: all aesthetic practitioners have the same training. Let me explain
items.script:
Training varies a great deal. Some practitioners come from a medical background, such as nursing, dentistry, medicine or pharmacy. Others arrive through courses of different lengths.

There is no single route, and that is why asking matters. You can ask about their background, how long they have practised, who supervises them and what they do if something goes wrong.

A confident, qualified practitioner enjoys these questions. They will show you certificates, explain their insurance and tell you who they refer to when needed.

A few quick checks help: ask whether they hold a recognised healthcare qualification, whether they carry insurance, and whether they keep up with training. Look at how they talk about safety, and whether they welcome questions. Their answers tell you more than a glossy brochure or an Instagram feed.

What would you ask a practitioner about their background? Tell me and I will answer.

items.hook: "Cheaper is the same, surely?" What sits behind a price
items.script:
A price covers more than the treatment in your face. It covers the consultation, the qualified practitioner, the quality of the product, the insurance, the aftercare and the follow up if you need it.

When a price looks unusually low, I ask what has been left out. It might be the product, the time, the training or the support afterwards.

Value matters. You can find fair prices at clinics that do all of this properly, so I encourage you to ask what is included before you decide.

Cheaper clinics can be wonderful, and some are run by excellent practitioners with lower overheads. The key is to ask what is included and who treats you. A fair price from a safe, honest practitioner beats a bargain from someone who cannot answer your questions, and you are welcome to compare.

What does your ideal price include? Tell me, and I will say whether that is realistic.

items.hook: Myth: you need to be unhappy with your looks to have a treatment
items.script:
Many of my patients feel happy with themselves. They are curious about small refinements, or they want to look as rested as they feel.

Others are going through a life change and want to feel like themselves again. And some come to ask a question and leave with a skincare plan.

You never need a reason that sounds dramatic. A calm, thoughtful motivation is perfectly welcome here.

Some of my happiest patients have said, I did not need it, I just wanted it. That is a perfectly good reason, provided it comes from a calm place. I ask a few gentle questions, we talk about options and the pace, and you decide with a clear head. Wanting something is a good enough start.

I always ask what is behind a request, because it helps me guide you well. What brought you to thinking about it?

items.hook: "Won't my skin get worse if I stop?" Let me explain
items.script:
Your skin carries on ageing at its own pace, with or without treatment. When a treatment wears off, your face gradually returns to how it would have looked anyway.

Stopping does not make things worse than before. Some people feel it looks different because they have grown used to a refreshed look, and that feeling is natural.

I talk about this at every consultation, so you understand how treatments behave over time and feel in charge of the next step.

I often compare it to a haircut grown out. The style fades, and your hair carries on growing as it always did. Looking after your skin with sun protection and good habits will serve you whatever you decide. I am always happy to talk through what to expect if you pause or stop.

What would you like to know about stopping? Ask me anything.

items.hook: Myth: social media filters show what treatments can do
items.script:
Filters smooth, brighten and reshape in ways no treatment can match. They also make everything look flawless from every angle.

Real faces have texture, asymmetry and personality, and that is how we recognise people. When I plan with a patient, I work with what you have and what is realistic for you.

If a filtered photo inspired you, bring it, and we will talk about what lies behind the feeling. Sometimes it is a wish for glowing skin. Sometimes it is a worry about tired eyes.

Filters also change the lighting and the angle, which can make a face look entirely different. The camera can add shine, hide texture and change proportions. Real life looks warmer and more varied. I encourage patients to judge by how they feel in the mirror at home, in ordinary light.

Which filter have you caught yourself smiling at? Tell me in the comments.

items.hook: Do treatments really last "forever"? An honest timeline
items.script:
Aesthetic treatments are temporary. Different treatments last different lengths of time, and your own body, lifestyle and habits influence that too.

At your consultation, I explain how long a particular treatment usually lasts, what changes gradually and when a review would be sensible. If anyone tells you something lasts forever, ask them for the evidence.

Planning for the long run helps you budget, decide and relax. I like patients to hear the whole picture before they begin.

Lifestyle matters too. Sun exposure, smoking, sleep and stress all shape how long a result seems to last. I talk through those factors honestly, and I give you a rough range. Planning with a range lets you budget and decide with confidence.

Would you like me to explain how a treatment ages with you? Ask in the comments.

items.hook: Myth: it is only for women. I treat all sorts of faces
items.script:
My chair welcomes everyone. Men, women and non-binary patients all come for consultations, and their reasons are as varied as they are.

Some want to look less tired at work. Some want to feel more confident for an event. Some are curious and simply want to chat.

I plan each face on its own merits, because features, expressions and goals differ from person to person.

Men sometimes tell me they feel a little awkward booking, and I always say they need not. Quiet appointments, discreet communication and straightforward advice are standard in my clinic. My aim is for every patient to feel respected, whoever they are and whatever brought them through the door.

If you have wondered whether you would be welcome, you would be. What would help you feel comfortable coming in?

items.hook: "My partner will not like it." Who is this for, really?
items.script:
This one comes up often, and it is tender. Your face belongs to you, and so does the decision.

It can help to talk it through with the people you love. Many partners are supportive once they hear the reasons. Some feel unsure at first and come round after a conversation.

I ask every patient who they are doing it for. The best reasons are yours alone, such as feeling comfortable, confident or more like yourself.

Sometimes it helps to write down your reasons before you decide. Are they yours? Do they feel calm and kind? If you cannot answer clearly, wait. I would rather you take another week than commit to something you feel unsure about. The right decision stands up to a few quiet days.

If it helps, bring your partner to a consultation and ask your questions together. Who in your life has views on this? Tell me how they feel.

items.hook: Myth: a treatment will fix everything about my face
items.script:
No single treatment does that, and I would be doing you a disservice if I implied otherwise.

Treatments address particular concerns, such as a specific line, a loss of volume or a patch of skin. Everyday habits, skincare, sleep, sun protection and general health all contribute, and they shape what you see in the mirror.

I like to look at the whole picture with you, and sometimes the simplest step makes the biggest difference.

I also remind patients that confidence comes from many places, such as friendships, work, health and rest. A treatment can be a lovely addition. It sits alongside everything else and works best when you feel well in other ways too. I like to look at the whole picture with you.

What would you most like to see change? Tell me, and I will tell you what is realistic.

items.hook: "Will people judge me?" Here is what I hear from patients
items.script:
Many of the people in my chair worry about this, and I understand.

Most patients tell me nobody has said anything unkind. A few tell me a friend asked for my number. Some keep their treatment private, and that is entirely their choice. I respect your privacy and I never share your details.

My clinic is a judgement free room. I care about how you feel and how you look after, and I leave opinions at the door.

I also keep my waiting area private and my schedule gentle, so you rarely see another patient. If you prefer a quieter time of day, I will happily offer it. Little details like that help people relax, and they let you focus on your own appointment without worrying about being seen.

Who are you worried will judge? Tell me, and let us think about it together.

items.hook: Myth: you can only get great results in London
items.script:
Excellent care exists in towns and cities across the country. What matters is the practitioner's training, the clinic's standards and the care you receive.

Local clinics offer something valuable. You can pop back for a review, see the same person every time and build a relationship over the years.

Travelling for an appointment can mean a trickier follow up if you have a question. I always encourage patients to think about aftercare when choosing where to go.

When you travel, ask what happens if you need a review. A practitioner who works nearby can see you quickly and know your history. Distance matters less than communication, though, so choose someone who answers messages promptly and gives clear aftercare. That reliability counts for a great deal.

Where do you live? Tell me, and I will tell you what to look for nearby.

items.hook: "Do I have to tell my family?" Privacy in the treatment room
items.script:
You choose who knows. Your appointments, notes and photographs are confidential, and I never share them without your written consent.

Some patients are happy to chat about it over Sunday lunch. Others keep it entirely to themselves. Both are fine, and I plan around your preference, including how and when I contact you.

If you want discretion, tell me at booking and I will make sure you have it. You deserve a space where you feel safe to ask questions.

I also keep my messages short and non specific, such as a simple reminder with the time, so a glance at your phone reveals nothing. Tell me how you like me to contact you, and I will follow that. Discretion is easy to arrange once I know what suits you.

How private would you like your appointment to be? Tell me, and we will arrange it.

items.hook: Myth: bruising is guaranteed. What actually helps
items.script:
Some people bruise and many do not. It depends on your body, the area treated and a few everyday factors.

Before an appointment, I ask you to avoid certain things like alcohol and some supplements, because they can raise the chance. I work carefully, apply gentle pressure and give you aftercare advice to help.

If a mark appears, it normally fades over days. Concealer and patience help, and I always suggest keeping your diary clear of big events for a couple of weeks.

Arnica and similar remedies get mentioned a lot, and I am happy to talk about what the evidence says. Keeping your head raised and avoiding heat helps. Most marks are harmless and settle, and I check on you afterwards so you are never left wondering.

Have you got an event coming up? Tell me the date and I will help you plan.

items.hook: "Will I look different on the day?" What the first week looks like
items.script:
Right after a treatment, some people notice redness, small bumps or swelling that settles. These are common and often fade within hours or days, depending on the treatment.

Final changes take longer to appear, which is why I schedule a review and judge once things have settled. You might feel a bit self conscious in the first few days, and that is normal too.

I talk through what to expect, I send written aftercare and I stay available if something worries you.

Mild tenderness and small bumps are common, and I explain which signs are ordinary and which call for a phone call. I give you my number and tell you when I will check in. That plan makes the first week feel manageable, and it replaces guesswork with calm information.

What would you like to do in the week after a treatment? Tell me, and I will plan around it.

items.hook: Myth: the more you have done, the better you look. The sweet spot is smaller
items.script:
More rarely means better. A refined result comes from careful choices, spaced sensibly, with time to review.

I use the smallest effective approach first, then see how it settles. Most people find that gentle steps give a lovely, believable result, and they save money too.

Anyone who suggests everything at once deserves a pause. Good planning has patience built in.

Slow and steady also keeps your options open. If you want to add something later, you can. If you prefer to stop, you can. A measured approach respects your budget and your timeline, and it gives your face a chance to settle so we judge the result accurately.

If you ever feel pressured to add more, trust your instincts and say you will think about it. What does a sensible pace look like to you?

items.hook: "I read something scary online." Let us go through it calmly
items.script:
The internet can be a worrying place, and I understand why searches lead to anxiety.

Bring what you read to your consultation. I will go through it with you, explain what is accurate and what is exaggerated, and tell you the real risks for the treatment we are discussing. Every treatment carries some, and you deserve to hear them clearly.

Then we talk about how I reduce those risks, what to watch for afterwards and who to call.

I also suggest choosing a reliable source, such as a professional body or your practitioner, over a forum thread. Online stories tend to feature the dramatic cases, and quiet, uneventful experiences rarely get shared. A balanced picture requires context, and I am happy to supply it.

Knowledge settles nerves. What did you read that stuck with you? Tell me, and I will answer.

items.hook: Myth: skincare cannot make a difference. Here is where it shines
items.script:
Good skincare matters a great deal, and it works alongside any treatment I offer.

Sun protection every day is the single most useful habit for your skin. A gentle cleanser, a suitable moisturiser and a considered routine help with hydration, texture and comfort.

Many patients start with a simple plan and see their skin look healthier before they consider anything else. It also helps treatments last, so the two work together.

I enjoy helping patients build a simple routine that fits their budget. A cleanser, a moisturiser and a daily sun cream cover the essentials, and we can add something targeted if your skin needs it. Starting small is a very good plan.

What does your current routine look like? Tell me, and I will suggest one small change.

items.hook: "I don't want to look like a celebrity." Good, neither do I
items.script:
Wonderful, because I want you to look like you.

I never use celebrity faces as a template. Your face has its own proportions, its own character and its own story. A thoughtful plan builds on those, and my job is to protect the things that make you recognisable.

Bring an idea of the mood you like, such as fresh, rested or polished, and we will talk about how that might work on your features.

Celebrity photos are usually edited, lit by professionals and styled by teams. They show a polished version of a person, far removed from breakfast time. I would rather help you find your own best version, which looks wonderful in real life and in ordinary light.

Who inspires you? Tell me, and we will explore what you like about them.

items.hook: Myth: a treatment on your lunch break leaves no trace. The honest version
items.script:
Some treatments have little downtime and some leave redness, swelling or bruising for a few days.

Planning matters. I recommend choosing a quieter day if you are attending an important event, and I give guidance on what to expect for your particular treatment.

Lunch breaks work for some quick procedures, and I tell you honestly when you would be better off waiting for a calmer week.

Some of my patients plan treatments on a Friday so the weekend takes care of any redness. Others book a few weeks before an event to leave plenty of time for settling. I help you pick the date that suits your diary, and I explain what to expect for your specific treatment.

When is your next big event? Tell me, and I will tell you how to time things.

items.hook: "Is it safe?" The questions I answer before every treatment
items.script:
Every treatment has risks, and I explain them clearly before we begin. Safety comes from training, a thorough health history, quality products, a clean working environment and honest aftercare.

I tell you what side effects can occur, how common they are and what to do if something concerns you. I record everything in your notes, and you leave with my contact details.

If I feel a treatment would be unsafe for you, I say so and suggest another route.

Before any treatment, I check your identity, review your consent and confirm what we agreed. I wash my hands, prepare a clean workspace and open products in front of you. These steps may look small, and together they form the backbone of safe practice.

What worries you most about safety? Tell me, and I will answer properly.

items.hook: Myth: only the vain have aesthetic treatments. Meet my real patients
items.script:
My patients include teachers, nurses, farmers, grandmothers, new mums, retirees and business owners.

They come for all kinds of reasons. A tired face after a hard year. A wish to feel confident at work. A milestone birthday. Pure curiosity.

Wanting to feel good in your skin is a kind thing to want. You can care about how you look and care about everything else too.

Some people tell me they feel shy about telling friends. Others shout it from the rooftops. There is no right way. What matters is that you feel comfortable and cared for. I never assume a reason, and I enjoy hearing yours when you feel like sharing it.

What brought you to thinking about it? Tell me your reason.

items.hook: "Will it stay put or migrate?" What I tell patients about filler
items.script:
Dermal filler is placed carefully at the right depth, and a well planned treatment is designed to sit where it was put. Over time the body gradually absorbs it.

Placement, amount, product choice and your own anatomy all matter, and so does having a trained practitioner. I tell you what to expect, I assess you at review and I discuss dissolving options where appropriate.

If you have seen alarming photos online, bring them to your consultation, and we will talk about what went wrong in those cases.

Choosing a reputable product, placing it at the right depth and using a sensible amount all reduce risks. I also keep up with safety updates and know how to manage unwanted results. If you ever have a concern, contact me promptly, since early help makes a real difference.

What concerns you about filler? Tell me, and I will explain.

items.hook: Myth: you will be pressured into buying. What I do instead
items.script:
I run my consultations as conversations. I explain, I suggest and I leave decisions with you.

I never use countdown clocks, last chance messages or pushy follow ups. If you want to book, I welcome it. If you want to go away and think, I welcome that too.

Patients tell me this is the part they appreciate most. You deserve a decision made with a clear head.

If I recommend a follow up, I explain why, and I tell you it is optional. There is no obligation to purchase, and you can decline anything I suggest. The consultation exists to inform you, and the choice always rests with you.

Have you ever felt pressured in a clinic? Tell me how that felt.

items.hook: The myth I would retire first: "good aesthetics means a changed face"
items.script:
Good aesthetics means a face that looks like you on your best day.

It values proportion, expression, skin health and the way you feel in your own reflection. A skilled practitioner holds back more often than they add, and they respect the character in a face.

Some of the loveliest outcomes I see are barely noticeable to anyone except the patient. People simply say that you look well.

I often say that if people notice your treatment, I have done too much. If they say you look well and cannot say why, we are on the right track. That quiet outcome makes me prouder than any dramatic transformation, and it suits most patients far better.

What would looking well mean for you? Tell me, and we will start there.

title: Straight Answers
description: Thirty scripts that answer the questions patients are too polite to ask.

items.hook: How much does a treatment cost? Here is how I explain pricing
items.script:
Prices depend on the treatment, the amount needed, the product and the time involved. I give you a clear figure in your consultation, in writing, before you decide.

I explain what is included, such as the consultation, the treatment, the aftercare and any review appointment. If a recommended plan has several steps, I show the total and the order, so you can choose what to do first.

If a price feels high, I can suggest a different approach or a staged plan. Nobody should feel awkward about asking.

Some patients like to begin with the consultation fee, then decide on treatment afterwards. Others prefer a rough guide beforehand. I am happy to give ranges over the phone so you can plan, and I always confirm the exact figure in writing at your appointment.

What would you like to know about costs? Ask me in the comments.

items.hook: How long does a treatment appointment take? Plan around this
items.script:
Most treatments take between fifteen and forty five minutes, plus time for preparation and aftercare advice. Allow an hour for the whole visit, so you do not feel rushed.

Some procedures take longer, and I tell you at booking. I also build in time for questions, photographs and consent.

Aim to arrive a few minutes early with a clean face and a calm mind. Then leave yourself a quiet half hour afterwards if you can.

If it is your first visit, I suggest allowing extra time. We can chat, take photographs and complete forms without anyone looking at a watch. Nervous patients often say a relaxed start made the rest of the visit easier, and I agree wholeheartedly.

What does your diary look like this month? Tell me, and I will help you find a good slot.

items.hook: Can I drive and go back to work after my appointment?
items.script:
In most cases, yes. Many treatments need little recovery, and patients return to their day straight afterwards.

You might notice redness, small bumps or slight swelling. If your work involves meeting people, think about whether a bit of colour in the face matters to you. I explain what to expect for your particular treatment, and I advise on timing.

For anything with more downtime, I say so clearly and help you plan.

Wear a hat or scarf if you wish, and bring sunglasses on a bright day. Some patients apply a little mineral make up once I say it is fine. I will give you tailored advice for your treatment, including when it is safe to wear make up again.

What do you do for work? Tell me, and I will tell you how to fit it around your day.

items.hook: What should I avoid before my appointment? A simple list
items.script:
Avoid alcohol for about a day beforehand, since it can raise the chance of bruising. Check with me about blood thinning medicines and supplements such as fish oil, vitamin E and ginkgo, and never stop a prescribed medicine without speaking to your doctor.

Skip strong skincare ingredients, sunbeds and facials for a few days before. Arrive well hydrated, and tell me if you have a cold sore, a fever or an infection.

I send a specific list with your booking, based on your treatment.

It also helps to avoid anti inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen unless your doctor has prescribed them, because they can increase bruising. Paracetamol is usually fine. Always check with your doctor or pharmacist, and let me know what you take so I can advise properly.

Would you like me to send you mine? Message me and I will share it.

items.hook: What should I do after my treatment? Your first twenty four hours
items.script:
Keep your skin clean, and avoid touching the area. Skip strenuous exercise, heat such as saunas and sunbeds, and alcohol for the period I recommend. Sleep with your head slightly raised if I suggest it.

Follow the written aftercare I give you, because it is specific to your treatment. Take photos if you like, since they help at your review.

If something worries you, call me. I would much prefer a phone call to a night of wondering.

Over the next few days, keep an eye on the area and take notes about anything unusual. Sleep well, drink water and give yourself a quiet evening. Small acts of kindness to yourself support healing and make the first night feel peaceful.

What helps you feel looked after after an appointment? Tell me, and I will build it in.

items.hook: When will I see the final result? A realistic timeline
items.script:
It depends on the treatment. Some changes appear within days, some take a couple of weeks and some build gradually.

That is why I book a review at around two weeks for many treatments. By then, swelling has settled and we can assess the outcome fairly.

I explain the timeline at your consultation so you know what to expect, and I suggest keeping your diary calm before big events.

Patience helps. Many patients feel a flicker of doubt around day three, when swelling is at its peak, and it settles beautifully by the review. I send a reminder before your appointment so you remember to take comparison photos in good light.

Have you got a date in mind? Tell me, and I will work backwards from it.

items.hook: How often should I come back? Here is how I plan it
items.script:
There is no universal answer. It depends on the treatment, how your body responds and what you want.

Some patients return every few months. Others come once a year, or take a long break. I review you each time and suggest a sensible interval based on how things have settled.

You choose how often to come back, and I would rather see you less often with a result you love.

We also think about the pattern of your life, such as holidays, events and budgets. Spacing visits around those makes treatments feel manageable. If you ever want a break, take one. I am happy to welcome you back whenever you are ready.

How often do you picture visiting? Tell me, and I will tell you what is realistic.

items.hook: What if I'm unhappy with the result? My process
items.script:
Tell me. That is the first step, and I want to hear it.

We arrange a review. I look at the area with you, in the same light as before, and I listen to what bothers you. Some things settle with time. Some can be adjusted, and in some cases there are options to reverse or soften a result.

I keep notes of everything, and I will always take your concern seriously. A good practitioner stays with you through the awkward bits.

I record my notes, your photographs and the plan we agree. If you decide the result is not for you, we discuss options and costs openly, with no awkwardness. I would much prefer you to be happy than politely silent, and I welcome the conversation.

Has a clinic ever brushed off your concerns? Tell me how it went.

items.hook: Can I have treatments while pregnant or breastfeeding?
items.script:
Many aesthetic treatments are not recommended during pregnancy or while breastfeeding, simply because there is not enough safety evidence. I ask about both in every consultation.

If you are pregnant or planning to be, tell me. We can wait, and we can focus on gentle skincare in the meantime. Plenty of patients return after their baby arrives, once they feel ready.

Your wellbeing and your baby's come first, and I would never take a risk to fit a diary slot.

Skincare can still be gentle and effective during these months, and I am happy to suggest safe options. Chat with your midwife or doctor if you have questions. When you feel ready again, I will be delighted to see you for a fresh consultation.

Are you planning a family? Tell me, and I will help you plan around it.

items.hook: What is the difference between a nurse, a doctor and a dentist doing aesthetics?
items.script:
All three can be well qualified, and what matters is the individual's training, experience and standards.

Doctors, dentists and nurses all learn about anatomy, safety and patient care in their main careers. Some prescribers can prescribe medicines directly, and nurses can work with an independent prescriber for certain treatments.

Ask any practitioner about their aesthetics training, their insurance and who prescribes. A good one answers with a smile.

I explain my own route in plain terms and offer to show you my certificates. Ask about their prescriber too, since many treatments require a prescription from a qualified professional. A practitioner who answers openly is showing you how they handle responsibility.

Do you have a preference? Tell me what matters to you in a practitioner.

items.hook: What is a medical consultation really for? Three reasons
items.script:
First, safety. I check your health history, medications and allergies before anything else.

Second, suitability. Not every treatment suits every person, and a consultation helps me advise honestly.

Third, understanding. You learn what a treatment involves, what it costs, how it feels and what to expect after. By the end you can decide with a clear head.

Some treatments legally require a consultation before they can be prescribed, which is another good reason to have one.

I also use the consultation to talk through the aftercare, the costs and the possible risks. By the end you have a written plan and a clear sense of what each step involves. The best consultations leave patients wanting to ask even more questions next time.

Which of these matters most to you? Tell me, and let us begin there.

items.hook: Do I need a patch test? When and why I recommend one
items.script:
For some treatments and skincare products, a patch test helps check for reactions before using them more widely.

I apply a tiny amount in a discreet area and observe the skin over the following days. If your skin reacts, we choose something different.

It adds a short step and it protects you. Patients with sensitive skin or a history of allergies often benefit most.

It takes a day or two to see how your skin responds, and I tell you what signs to watch for. Mild redness can be ordinary, while itching, swelling or blistering call for a phone call. A short wait gives us far more confidence about what suits you.

Have you ever reacted to a product? Tell me what happened, and I will take it into account.

items.hook: What can I wear and do the day after a treatment?
items.script:
You can usually wear loose, comfortable clothes, and you may want to avoid anything that rubs the treated area. Wash your hair gently and avoid hot showers if I have asked you to.

Skip heavy exercise, saunas and sunbeds for a short time, and wear sun protection every day. Make up usually waits a little while, depending on the treatment.

I give you a card with the precise guidance for your appointment, and you can message me if you have a question.

Your pillow matters too. A fresh, clean pillowcase is a lovely idea, and sleeping on your back helps keep pressure off the treated area for the first night. Little habits like these support healing and cost nothing.

What does your schedule look like tomorrow? Tell me, and I will help you plan.

items.hook: How do I find a good practitioner near me? A short guide
items.script:
Look for someone with a healthcare background or a regulated registration, for example nursing, dentistry or medicine. Check their insurance, and ask about training and supervision.

Look at their reviews and how they respond to questions. Visit the clinic, and see whether it feels clean, calm and welcoming. Ask for a consultation before you commit.

Trust your gut. If a clinic rushes you, avoids questions or pushes you to book, walk away politely.

Another quick check is to look at their consultation process. A thorough one covers your history, your goals and your questions before any treatment is offered. If a clinic suggests treating on arrival, take that as a signal to pause and ask more.

Where would you start looking? Tell me, and I will add to the list.

items.hook: Can I have treatments with my medical condition? A careful conversation
items.script:
Many people with long term conditions can have aesthetic treatments, and some cannot, or need extra care. It depends on the condition, your medication and how well controlled it is.

Tell me everything at your consultation. Sometimes I will ask for a letter or a word with your GP before we go ahead. That is part of looking after you properly.

Your health always comes first, and I would rather say wait than risk it.

Some conditions need extra thought, such as autoimmune conditions, bleeding disorders, diabetes and a history of keloid scarring. None of these automatically rule you out. It simply means we plan carefully and sometimes involve your doctor. Honest information helps me keep you safe.

What questions do you have about your own health? Tell me, and we will go through them.

items.hook: What is the difference between a clinic and a salon for aesthetics?
items.script:
Clinics often have medical oversight, clinical standards and a working environment designed for safe treatments. Salons offer beauty therapies, and some also offer more advanced treatments with their own safeguards.

What matters most is the qualification of the person treating you, the cleanliness of the room and the quality of the aftercare.

Ask what regulation covers the clinic, and ask who is responsible if something goes wrong. A good place will answer clearly.

Cleanliness, supervision and clear procedures matter wherever you go. Visit before you book, notice how the staff talk to each other and ask who is responsible for your care. A thoughtful answer reveals a lot about the way a place is run.

Where do you feel most comfortable having treatments? Tell me.

items.hook: How do I know a product is genuine? Questions worth asking
items.script:
Ask what the product is, who makes it and where the practitioner buys it. A professional can show you the packaging, the batch number and the expiry date.

I record those details in your notes, so there is a clear trail if you ever need it. Be wary of unusually low prices and anyone who cannot name their supplier.

You deserve to know exactly what goes into your face.

I keep my product packaging and batch details in your notes, and I can show you the boxes on request. Genuine suppliers provide paperwork, and a good practitioner welcomes questions. If you ever feel unsure, take a photo of the label and ask me about it.

Have you ever asked a clinic about their products? Tell me how it went.

items.hook: Can I exercise after my treatment? Here is the plan I give patients
items.script:
Gentle walking is usually fine. Strenuous exercise, saunas, steam rooms and hot yoga often wait for a day or two, depending on the treatment, because heat and increased blood flow can affect the area.

I give you a specific timeframe at your appointment, and I write it down. It is a short pause and it helps the treatment settle well.

If you love your gym class, plan your appointment for the start of a quieter week.

After the pause, you can ease back in with gentle activity and build up. Listen to your body. If anything feels sore or warm, rest a little longer and send me a message. Your routine will return quickly, and the skin appreciates the break.

What is your favourite way to exercise? Tell me, and I will plan around it.

items.hook: What is a cooling off period and why do I give you one?
items.script:
It is a gap between your consultation and your treatment, so you can reflect on your decision. Some treatments require this by law, and I offer it for others too.

The idea is to protect you from making choices in the moment. You can sleep on it, read the information, talk to people you trust and book when you feel certain.

It can feel slow, and most patients tell me they feel relieved afterwards.

Even for treatments without a legal requirement, I like to offer reflection time because it improves decisions. Patients have told me it takes pressure off and lets them enjoy the process. A gentle pause shows respect for the choice you are making.

Would you like a day or a week to think? Tell me which suits you.

items.hook: How do I look after my skin between appointments?
items.script:
Wear sun protection every day, even in winter. Cleanse gently, moisturise suitably for your skin type and drink enough water. Sleep well when you can, and be kind about stress.

Introduce new products one at a time so you can spot reactions. Avoid picking, and book a skin check if something changes.

A small daily routine does more than an occasional big one. I can suggest a simple plan for your skin.

If your skin changes suddenly, such as a new mole, a patch that will not heal or a rash, please see your GP or a dermatologist. I am happy to look and advise, and I will always refer on when something needs medical attention. Your health comes first.

What is in your routine right now? Tell me, and I will tweak it.

items.hook: Do men get treatments too? Yes, and here is what they ask
items.script:
A growing number of my patients are men, and their questions are wonderfully practical. How obvious will it be? How long before I can go back to work? Will I still look like me?

I take the same careful approach with every face. I look at structure, expression and goals, and I suggest a plan that respects your features. Men's faces often have stronger bone structure and different ageing patterns, so I plan accordingly.

You are always welcome, and the room is relaxed.

Some men prefer early morning or lunchtime appointments, and I arrange those. I also keep communication discreet, and I answer questions in plain language. Whatever your reason for asking, you are welcome here and your questions are taken seriously.

What would you like to ask? Tell me, and I will answer plainly.

items.hook: Can I combine treatments in one visit? What I consider
items.script:
Sometimes yes and sometimes it is wiser to space them out. I consider safety, your recovery, how each treatment behaves and how you would like to feel afterwards.

Combining can save time. Spacing can make it easier to see what each treatment does and to adjust if needed.

At your consultation, I explain my reasoning and lay out options. You choose what suits your life.

I sometimes suggest a quiet gap of a couple of weeks between treatments so we can see how each one settles. That lets me fine tune the next step, and it gives you time to enjoy the first result. Planning in stages is often kinder to your face and your budget.

Which feels easier for you, one visit or several? Tell me, and I will plan around it.

items.hook: Will my insurance or GP know? The privacy answer
items.script:
Your aesthetic treatments are your own business. I keep your records confidential and I only share them with your written consent, unless the law requires otherwise or your safety depends on it.

If you have a medical condition, I may ask to speak with your GP, and I do that only with your permission.

I explain my privacy policy at your consultation and I answer any questions about where your information lives.

Your insurer or employer has no access to my records, and I do not provide them with any information. If you ever need a letter for medical reasons, I discuss it with you first. Knowing how your information is handled helps you feel secure.

What would help you feel safe sharing your details? Tell me.

items.hook: Can I have a treatment during a cold, illness or after a vaccine?
items.script:
If you feel unwell, please reschedule. Treating when your body is busy fighting something can raise the chance of a reaction and makes it harder to assess results.

After vaccinations, many clinics suggest a short gap, and I give guidance at booking. If you have a cold sore or an infection near the area, we wait.

A short delay costs very little and protects your wellbeing.

After a vaccine, I usually suggest waiting a couple of weeks so any reaction can be recognised clearly. After a cold or flu, I wait until you feel completely well. These pauses are short and wise, and they keep your appointment safe and comfortable.

If you are unsure, message me. I would rather answer a question than treat in doubt. Are you feeling well today?

items.hook: What should I ask on the phone before booking?
items.script:
Ask who will treat you and what their qualifications are. Ask whether a consultation comes first and whether it costs anything.

Ask what the aftercare involves and who to call if you have a concern. Ask about their insurance and how they store your information.

Listen for a warm, clear answer. A good clinic welcomes these calls and enjoys them.

You can also ask about the clinic's cancellation policy, parking and opening hours. Practical questions help you plan, and they show how organised the clinic is. A good receptionist or practitioner will answer warmly and clearly.

Feel free to message me with yours, and I will answer. What is on your list?

items.hook: Will treatments interact with my medication or supplements?
items.script:
They can. Some medicines and supplements change how your body reacts, for example by affecting bruising, healing or the safety of certain treatments.

That is why I ask for a full list at your consultation, including prescription medicines, over the counter products, vitamins and herbal supplements. Please do not stop any prescribed medication without speaking with your doctor.

I check each item and advise you on timing.

Some everyday supplements, like fish oil and vitamin E, can increase bruising. Certain prescription medicines affect healing or clotting. I will tell you when to stop or hold off, and I will always suggest checking with your doctor before changing anything.

Could you jot down your list tonight? Tell me one thing on it that surprised you.

items.hook: What should my skin look like before I start?
items.script:
Your skin can be perfectly ordinary, and healthy skin responds best to treatment. I look for skin that is free from infection, irritation and open sores, and I like to see sun protection in your daily routine.

If your skin is inflamed, sunburnt or reacting to a product, we pause and calm it first. A short skincare plan often helps.

Tell me about your skin at your consultation, and I will advise you on the best starting point.

A good skincare routine helps skin prepare, and I may suggest a few weeks of gentle care first. Hydrated, well protected skin heals better and looks happier afterwards. It is a lovely way to begin and often brings a visible lift by itself.

What is your skin doing right now? Tell me.

items.hook: How do I tell if I'm being upsold? Three signs to watch
items.script:
First, the plan keeps growing. A genuine recommendation matches your goals, and an upsell adds extras you did not mention.

Second, the clock appears. Offers that vanish tonight or last slots left create pressure, and good care rarely needs it.

Third, the questions dry up. If your practitioner stops asking about your goals and starts talking about packages, pause.

An honest plan can include rest periods, review points and the option to stop. If a clinic offers discounts that vanish at the end of the appointment, take a breath. A fair offer will still be fair after a night's sleep, and you will feel better for choosing calmly.

A confident practitioner is happy for you to go home and think. Have you ever felt upsold? Tell me how it felt.

items.hook: Can I take photos and share my treatment online?
items.script:
You can, and it is entirely up to you. I would suggest thinking about privacy and timing, since your face may look different in the first few days.

If I would like to use your photos in my own content, I ask for your written consent and explain exactly where they will appear. You can say no, and you can change your mind later.

I follow advertising rules carefully, so I avoid showing certain things and I never promise results.

Most clinics set their own policies, and the rules about advertising are strict, so you may notice a practitioner declining to repost your comments. That is part of following the guidelines. Your privacy and honesty stay at the centre of every decision I make.

Would you share it with friends? Tell me why or why not.

items.hook: The question nobody asks me, and I wish they would
items.script:
It is, what would you do if it were your own face?

I love that question because it invites honesty. My answer is usually thoughtful and modest. I might say that I would wait, or choose something simple, or look after my skin for a few months first.

It reminds me to treat every patient as I would treat someone I love.

I also ask patients what they would tell a friend who asked them the same thing. It brings out their instincts, and often their answer is wiser than mine. Honest questions lead to honest conversations, and I treasure them.

Next time you sit in a consultation, ask your practitioner. What does your gut say they would answer?
