title: Why Trust Me
description: Fifty scripts showing how you keep patients safe, informed and looked after.

items.hook: The safety checks I run before every single treatment
items.script:
Before I start, I confirm who you are and what we agreed. I review your health history for changes since last time and check for allergies, medication and any signs of infection near the area.

I wash my hands, put on fresh gloves and prepare a clean workspace. I check each product, its expiry date and its batch number. I clean your skin and mark the area if needed.

These steps take a few minutes, and they sit behind every careful treatment. You may spot them as small rituals, and I hope they reassure you.

I also ask you to confirm your name and date of birth aloud, and I read the plan back to you before I begin. A pause for questions comes right before the first touch. If you feel hesitant at any point, we stop and talk. These habits take about five minutes, and they give both of us a steady start. Over the years, they have caught small details more than once, which is exactly what they are for.

What would you like to see a practitioner do before they begin? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I always record batch numbers and what that means for you
items.script:
Every product has a batch number and an expiry date. I write both in your notes at every appointment.

If a manufacturer ever issues a safety notice, I can identify who received that batch and contact them quickly. You also have a clear record of what was used, which helps if you see another clinician in future.

It is a small piece of admin and it makes a real difference to your safety.

Batch records also help me notice patterns. If a patient has a reaction, I can check the details quickly and report it through the right channels. Good records are a quiet form of care, built from tiny habits repeated every single day. I would hope any clinic you visit follows a similar routine, and I encourage you to ask.

Would you like a copy of your treatment record? Ask me next time.

items.hook: The day I turned a patient away, and why I'm glad I did
items.script:
A patient came in determined to have a treatment, and her health history showed something that made it unsafe. We sat down, and I explained why I could not go ahead.

She was disappointed, and she was also grateful. We talked about alternatives, and she followed my advice about her skin. She later thanked me for being honest.

Saying no is part of the job, and it protects both of us.

Patients sometimes say they would have been furious, and then relieved. That tells me honesty matters even when it disappoints. I always follow a refusal with a phone call or message, so nobody leaves feeling dismissed. Where it helps, I suggest a doctor or another specialist who can look at the concern properly.

Would you want your practitioner to say no when needed? Tell me what you think.

items.hook: What emergency kit and training should a clinic have?
items.script:
A well run clinic keeps emergency equipment and medication for rare complications, and the team knows how to use it. They train regularly, keep their knowledge current and have a clear procedure.

You can ask about it politely at your consultation. A good practitioner is pleased you asked and will explain.

Most patients never need it, and having it ready is a sign of respect for your safety.

I check my equipment on a regular schedule and keep dates in a log. I also practise scenarios with colleagues so we respond calmly if something unexpected happens. Hopefully nobody ever needs it, and preparation is what lets me stay calm. A clinic that takes this seriously usually takes everything else seriously too.

Would you feel more confident knowing? Tell me.

items.hook: How I keep my clinic clean, behind the scenes
items.script:
I wipe down surfaces between patients, use single use items where appropriate and dispose of sharps safely. I wash my hands before and after every patient, and I wear fresh gloves for each one.

Equipment is cleaned and stored properly, and I check supplies regularly. The room is tidy and calm before you arrive.

These routines are largely invisible, and they matter greatly.

Cleaning is a routine I do between patients, and I do it in the same order every time. I also keep a record of my cleaning schedule and review it with my team. Patients rarely see these details, and I believe they should feel the benefit of them. A tidy, careful space is the base for every treatment.

What do you notice when you walk into a clinic? Tell me.

items.hook: What I do when a patient has a reaction
items.script:
First, I stay calm and look after you. I assess the situation, treat what I can and call for help if needed.

Then I record what happened and follow up with you. I explain what we know, what we will do and when I will check on you next. I stay in touch until you are comfortable.

Reactions are rare, and I take preparation seriously. It is the reason my training never stops.

I also keep emergency contact details at hand, and I know which services to call. In my notes, I record the time, the symptoms and the steps I took. I then review the case to see what I can learn. Honest reflection after a hard day helps me look after the next patient even better.

What would reassure you most in that moment? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I keep learning, even after years of practice
items.script:
Aesthetics keeps developing. New research appears, guidance updates and techniques evolve.

I attend training days, read journals and discuss cases with colleagues. I review my own work with fresh eyes and welcome feedback. It keeps my skills sharp and my judgement honest.

Patients benefit because I can offer informed advice.

I choose courses carefully, favouring those with supervised practice and a strong safety focus. I also join peer groups where we talk through tricky cases. Sharing experience makes everyone safer, and it keeps me curious. If a technique changes, I explain it to you in plain English and tell you why I adopted it.

When did you last learn something that changed your mind? Tell me.

items.hook: What it means that I am insured, and why you should ask
items.script:
Insurance protects you as well as me. If something goes wrong, appropriate cover supports compensation and care.

I carry professional indemnity insurance for the treatments I provide. I am happy to show you evidence, and you can ask any practitioner to do the same.

If someone avoids the question, that tells you plenty.

I renew my cover every year and keep the paperwork where I can find it. Insurance also tells you that a practitioner has been assessed for the treatments they carry out. If a treatment is not covered, a responsible practitioner will not offer it. Seeing the certificate takes thirty seconds, and it can bring real peace of mind.

Have you ever asked a clinic about insurance? Tell me how it went.

items.hook: How I decide a treatment is not right for you
items.script:
I listen first, then I weigh up your goals, your health, your face and your expectations. If a treatment would not give you what you hope for, I say so.

Other times safety decides it. A condition, a medicine or timing can make a treatment unwise.

I always explain my reasoning and offer another route, whether that is skincare, a different treatment or time.

Sometimes I suggest waiting until a health issue is settled, or until a medication changes. Other times, I recommend a different approach. I explain the reasons in everyday language and write them in your notes. Patients generally appreciate being told where the line is and why, and they often return when the time is right.

Would you like honest advice even when it means saying no? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I never rush a decision, even when the diary is full
items.script:
A full diary tempts any clinician to hurry, and I resist that. Rushing leads to mistakes and unhappy patients.

I keep my appointments long enough for conversation and care. I plan my day so I can give each person my full attention, and I leave gaps for questions.

That means I see fewer patients and I do a better job.

Unhurried appointments mean I can notice small details, like how you hold your jaw or when you pause before answering. Those details guide my advice. Quiet moments in the day also give me space to write careful notes. All of this helps me deliver safer, kinder care, and I think you can feel it in the room.

How does it feel when someone gives you proper time? Tell me.

items.hook: What a proper aftercare plan looks like
items.script:
It is written, specific and given to you before you leave. It explains what is normal, what to avoid and what to watch for.

It includes how to reach me, what to do in an emergency and when we will review the results. It reminds you of skincare and sun protection.

If a clinic gives you vague advice, ask for details. You deserve a plan.

It also tells you what to do if you cannot reach me, such as who to contact and when to seek urgent help. A proper aftercare plan reduces anxiety, because you have answers before you need them. I print it and also send it by message, so you always have a copy to hand.

What would you want written on yours? Tell me.

items.hook: How I handle your medical records and personal information
items.script:
I store your records securely and share them only with your consent, or when the law requires it. I limit who sees them, protect devices with passwords and keep paper notes locked away.

You have the right to ask what I hold and to request a copy. I explain this in plain English at your first visit.

Your trust in me includes your privacy, and I treat it that way.

I never leave notes on view, and I lock my screen whenever I step away. I use secure systems, and I share only what is necessary with other professionals. If you ever wish to withdraw consent or correct something, tell me, and I will deal with it promptly. You are in charge of your own information.

What would you like to know about your data? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I check your identity and age before treating you
items.script:
It protects you and the clinic. I confirm who you are, and I ensure every patient is over eighteen for aesthetic treatments.

It also keeps your records accurate, so I know exactly who received what. A friendly request for ID is a sign of a careful clinic.

I explain why I ask, and I keep the process polite and discreet.

Sometimes a younger friend comes along with a patient, and I explain politely that I can only treat adults. I never make anyone feel awkward about it. The rule protects young people while their faces and minds are still developing, and I am proud to hold it firmly.

Does it reassure you when a clinic checks? Tell me.

items.hook: What I look for in a supplier before I buy anything
items.script:
I buy only from reputable, licensed suppliers who can document their products. I check certification, storage conditions and traceability.

If a deal looks too good, I walk away. Cheap products can hide poor handling, doubtful origin or missing paperwork.

Your safety rests on the products I choose, and I choose with care.

I keep copies of invoices, certificates and batch information, and I store products as the manufacturer instructs. Reliable suppliers answer questions openly and provide proper paperwork. I would rather pay more and sleep well. If you ever see a clinic selling something that looks unusual, ask where it came from.

Do you ever wonder where products come from? Tell me what you would ask.

items.hook: How a good clinic handles complaints
items.script:
They listen, apologise where appropriate, investigate and respond in writing within a reasonable time. They explain what they found and what they will do.

A good clinic shares their complaints procedure and tells you who regulates them. They treat feedback as information.

If you ever have a concern, raise it. I would rather hear it directly and put it right.

I respond to complaints within a few days, and I keep records of every step. I also share what I learn with my team so we all improve. Patients who raise concerns help me look after others better. I thank them for it, even when the conversation is tough.

Would you feel comfortable making a complaint? Tell me what would help.

items.hook: Why I review my own results with a critical eye
items.script:
After each review appointment, I compare photos and notes. I ask myself what went well, what I could improve and what I would do differently.

I share my thoughts with you. If I see something I could do better, I tell you.

That habit keeps me honest and improves my work over time.

Sometimes I ask a colleague to look at my notes and share an honest opinion. Fresh eyes spot things I might miss. I also keep a list of questions to explore at my next training day. It keeps me humble and curious, and it means you benefit from my ongoing development.

Would you want your practitioner to be this open? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I limit how many treatments I will do in one day
items.script:
Tired hands make mistakes, and tired minds miss details. I cap my day so I can give each patient full attention.

I schedule breaks, keep the pace calm and avoid overbooking. It means a waiting list occasionally, and I think it is worth it.

Quality care takes energy, and I protect mine for your benefit.

I also build recovery time into my own week, with proper meals and a break each day. It sounds basic, and it protects my judgement and steadiness. Patients tell me my calm manner helps them relax. That calm is the result of a carefully planned schedule.

How do you feel about waiting for a good practitioner? Tell me.

items.hook: What a patient safety check looks like at your review
items.script:
At your review, I look at the treated area in the same light as before. I ask about any concerns, side effects or surprises, and compare photos.

I check your skin, ask how you feel and answer questions. If something needs attention, we discuss it straight away.

The review closes the loop and gives us both confidence.

If the review shows a concern, I make a plan and book a follow up. If everything looks good, I celebrate with you and set a date for the next check in, or nothing further. You always leave knowing what comes next, and you can contact me anytime between visits.

Do you like having a review booked? Tell me.

items.hook: Who regulates aesthetic practitioners? A short explainer
items.script:
It depends on your practitioner's background. Nurses, doctors, dentists and pharmacists belong to professional bodies with their own standards. Premises may be registered with local authorities, and some treatments fall under additional rules.

Advertising is regulated too, which is why you will not see me promoting prescription medicines directly.

Ask your practitioner who regulates them, and check the register if you want to.

You can usually find your practitioner on a professional register, which shows their qualifications and any conditions on their practice. Many clinics also display their registration with local authorities. Checking takes minutes, and it is a reassuring step before your first visit.

Would you like help finding the registers? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I only advertise what the rules allow
items.script:
UK advertising rules protect patients from misleading claims. Prescription only medicines cannot be advertised to the public, and claims must be honest and supportable.

That is why my posts talk about consultations, safety and care, and avoid before and after promises. It also means you hear honest information from me.

Compliance is part of respecting you.

That also means I explain things in a consultation that I would never put in a post. In the room, I can talk about your individual situation, your options and the right questions to ask. Online, I share general education and invitations to chat. Both are honest and appropriately careful.

Do you notice claims that sound too good? Tell me what stands out.

items.hook: Why I say "let me think about that" more than you might expect
items.script:
When a patient asks something I cannot answer with total confidence, I say so. Then I check, ask a colleague or look it up, and I come back to you.

I find that honesty lands well. Patients tell me it makes them trust the rest of what I say. Aesthetics involves many variables, and nobody knows everything about every face.

That pause protects you from a confident guess. It also shows I take your question seriously enough to get it right.

I keep a notebook of questions to follow up, and I often message patients later with what I found. They tell me it makes them feel valued, and I enjoy the research. Confidence in a practitioner grows when they are honest about what they do not yet know and willing to learn.

Ask me anything in the comments and I will either answer it or tell you when I will have an answer. What have you always wanted to know?

items.hook: What a good consent conversation sounds like
items.script:
It sounds like a chat. I explain what the treatment is, what it can do and what it cannot do. I describe the risks in plain language, including the rare ones, and the alternatives, including doing nothing.

I ask you to tell me in your own words what you understand, and I answer anything that is unclear. I give you time, and I give you written information to take home.

Only then do I ask you to sign, and you can still change your mind later.

I also ask you to repeat the key points in your own words, which tells me whether I explained clearly. If something sounds muddled, I try again with a simpler example. Consent should feel like understanding, and that takes patience and plenty of questions from both of us.

Have you had a consent conversation that felt thorough? Tell me about it.

items.hook: How I make sure the room is calm before you arrive
items.script:
I spend ten minutes before each appointment on the room. The lighting is soft, the surfaces are clean, the temperature is comfortable and the music is gentle. I lay out what I need so I am not rummaging while you wait.

Small touches matter. A blanket, a glass of water, a place to put your bag and a tissue within reach.

A calm room helps a nervous patient settle, and it helps me concentrate.

I keep a small tray with essentials in reach, so I do not have to leave your side during treatment. I check the lighting, the chair height and the room temperature. These tiny choices help me work steadily and keep you comfortable. A good atmosphere really does shape a treatment.

What helps you relax in a new place? Tell me, and I will try to add it.

items.hook: Why I always take a short break between patients
items.script:
It lets me reset. I wash my hands, tidy the room, review the next patient's notes and take a few slow breaths.

It means that each patient gets a fresh version of me, with my full attention. I do not carry yesterday's worries into today's treatment.

Patients rarely see these gaps, and they benefit from them. A rested practitioner is a safer practitioner.

I take a sip of water, stretch my shoulders and glance at the next patient's notes. Those two or three minutes keep me steady through a long day. Patients appreciate that I arrive at their appointment unhurried and ready to listen. Rest is part of safe, kind practice.

What helps you do your best work when you are busy? Tell me.

items.hook: How I explain risks without frightening you
items.script:
I tell you the truth, calmly and clearly. I explain what could happen, how likely it is and what we do about it. I use plain words, and I invite questions.

Most risks are small and manageable, and understanding them helps you feel in control. I never hide something to keep the mood light.

You should leave your consultation feeling informed, and I hope relieved to have heard it from someone you trust.

I use simple comparisons, like how likely a bruise is compared with how rare a serious reaction might be. I invite you to ask me to repeat anything. When you understand the odds and the plan, your worries usually shrink, and you can make a decision from a settled place.

Do you prefer to hear every detail or the headlines first? Tell me, and I will adapt.

items.hook: A time I changed my advice after listening to a patient
items.script:
A patient came in asking for one thing, and as she talked I realised her real worry sat somewhere else. She felt tired at work, and she thought a treatment would solve it.

We talked about sleep, stress and her skincare. She decided to start there, and she came back months later feeling brighter and more confident, with a much simpler plan.

Listening changed my advice, and it improved her experience.

After that appointment, I added a gentle question to my forms about what a patient hopes to feel. It helps me see past the first request. Listening for the reason behind the question often changes the plan entirely, and it nearly always makes it simpler and kinder.

Have you ever asked for one thing and needed another? Tell me.

items.hook: How to read reviews of an aesthetic clinic wisely
items.script:
Read a range of reviews, including the three and four star ones, since they often hold the most detail. Look for comments about communication, aftercare and honesty as well as results.

Notice how the clinic replies. A kind, professional answer to a criticism says plenty.

Be wary of a wall of identical five star reviews. Real feedback has variety.

Also look at dates. A steady flow of reviews over time suggests a clinic that cares about patients, while a sudden burst can look suspicious. Photos of the actual premises and staff add reassurance. Taking ten minutes to read thoughtfully can save you a lot of worry.

What do you look for in a review? Tell me, and I will add it.

items.hook: What happens if you need me after hours?
items.script:
I give every patient a way to reach me, such as a phone number or secure message, plus guidance on what is urgent. For anything that worries you, call me. If I cannot answer, I return your call as soon as I can, and I tell you where to go if you need urgent help.

Patients rarely use this, and they tell me knowing it exists helps them relax.

I explain out of hours arrangements at your appointment, so you know them before you need them. I also give you a list of symptoms that call for urgent medical help. You deserve to know where to turn at any time of day, and I am glad to give you that safety net.

How do you like to be contacted if you have a question? Tell me, and I will note it.

items.hook: Why I keep my appointment times generous
items.script:
Time lets me do three things well: listen, treat carefully and explain the aftercare. A rushed appointment squeezes all three.

I leave a buffer for the unexpected, such as an extra question, a nervous patient or a small adjustment. That buffer also means your appointment starts on time more often.

It costs me some income, and it gives you a better experience. I think it is the right trade.

A generous schedule also leaves room for a nervous patient who arrives early, or one who wants to talk before we begin. I would rather welcome you warmly than rush you in the door. That feeling of ease is part of the service, and I protect it carefully.

How long do you like an appointment to feel? Tell me.

items.hook: What a clear treatment plan includes
items.script:
A clear plan lists the treatments we discussed, the order, the timing and the expected cost. It describes the aim, the risks and the aftercare.

It records what you decided and what you want to think about. It tells you when we will review.

You should leave with a copy, so you can look at it calmly at home.

I also email you a copy so you can discuss it with a friend or partner. If your plans change, we update it together. Having it in writing keeps our conversation clear and protects both of us from misunderstandings. It takes a few minutes and means a great deal.

Would a written plan help you? Tell me, and I will happily prepare one.

items.hook: Why I will refer you to someone else when it is the right call
items.script:
Some concerns belong with a dermatologist, a GP, a dentist or a specialist. When I see something outside my scope, I say so and refer you.

It is part of caring for you properly. I would rather send you to the right person than treat something I should not.

Referring builds trust, and many patients return to me afterwards with gratitude.

I keep a short list of colleagues I trust, such as dermatologists, GPs, dentists and mental health professionals. When I refer someone, I explain why and offer to share relevant notes with their permission. Afterwards, I check in to see how things went. Collaboration keeps patients safe, and it reminds me that no single practitioner can do everything.

Have you ever been referred on? Tell me how it went.

items.hook: How I keep my skills sharp with practice and supervision
items.script:
I review cases with colleagues, attend refreshers and practise new techniques under supervision before I use them with patients. I keep notes on what I learn.

Good practitioners seek feedback and stay humble. I do both.

You benefit from a practitioner who keeps growing.

I also take time to read about new safety information and ask colleagues what they have seen in practice. A new technique has to prove itself before it reaches your face. Patients sometimes ask why I do not offer the latest trend, and my answer is usually that I am waiting for the evidence.

Do you like knowing your practitioner is still learning? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I never post patients' faces without permission
items.script:
Your face is yours. I ask for written consent before using any image, and I explain where it will appear and for how long. You can withdraw consent whenever you like.

I also follow advertising rules, which shape what I can show and say. It means my feed has plenty of conversation and little promise.

Privacy matters to me as much as results.

When I do ask permission, I show you exactly how I plan to use the photo and which details I will remove. You can say yes to one use and no to another. Many patients prefer to keep their treatment private, and I respect that wholeheartedly.

How would you feel about being asked? Tell me.

items.hook: What a clinic walk through tells you about standards
items.script:
Look at the reception, the treatment room and the way staff speak to each other. Is everything clean and tidy? Are sharps stored safely? Are consent forms and information leaflets available?

Do people greet you warmly and answer questions clearly? Is there a calm atmosphere?

These small signals reflect larger habits. You are welcome to ask for a tour before you book.

Pay attention to the paperwork too. Are your forms clear? Is your information stored securely? Is there a visible complaints procedure? Those details show a business that expects to be held accountable. A thoughtful clinic welcomes a curious patient, and I would encourage you to look around properly.

What do you notice first when you walk into a clinic? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I always follow up with a message the next day
items.script:
A short message the day after your treatment says, I am thinking of you. I ask how you feel, remind you of the aftercare and invite questions.

It takes a minute, and patients tell me it makes the world of difference. Worries shrink when someone asks.

I like knowing how my patients are doing, and I enjoy hearing the good news too.

It also gives me a chance to spot early signs of trouble, such as unusual swelling or discomfort, and to arrange a review. Patients often reply with a photo and a smile, and those messages brighten my morning. A few kind words can turn an anxious evening into a settled one.

Would you like a check in? Tell me how you prefer it, by text or by call.

items.hook: What good lighting does for an honest assessment
items.script:
Natural, even light shows the true shape and texture of your face. Harsh overhead lights, ring lights and filters distort shadows.

I assess you in consistent light at each visit, so comparisons are fair. I take photographs from the same angles, with the same expression.

It sounds fussy, and it protects you from misleading impressions.

Different lighting can make the same face look surprisingly different. A photograph near a window in the morning looks different from one in a dim room with an overhead bulb. When you compare progress, keep the light and angle consistent. It gives you a fair picture and keeps expectations realistic.

How do you look in your bathroom mirror compared to a window? Tell me what you notice.

items.hook: Why I tell patients to avoid big decisions on a bad day
items.script:
If you feel low, anxious or rushed, wait. A treatment will still be there next week.

Your mood colours how you see your reflection. On a hard day, small things feel enormous. On a calmer day, you can judge clearly.

I ask patients how they are feeling at the start of each visit, and I mean it. If the day is wobbly, we sometimes rebook.

I sometimes ask patients to keep a short diary of how they feel over a couple of weeks. It shows patterns, and it reveals whether a worry comes and goes. Clearer insight helps both of us decide whether to act or wait, and a calm mind is the best ally for any decision.

What helps you on tough days? Tell me, and I will keep it in mind.

items.hook: How to spot a clinic that cares about aftercare
items.script:
They explain it before you start. They give you written instructions, a contact number and a review date. They check in afterwards.

They answer questions kindly and keep notes. They treat problems as their responsibility.

If aftercare feels like an afterthought, ask more questions.

A good clinic also keeps records you can access, and it follows up if you do not attend a review. It explains what is normal and what is not, and it gives you a clear route to speak to a human. Aftercare is where a clinic shows its character.

You can also test it yourself. Message the clinic with a simple question about aftercare and notice how quickly and kindly they answer. A reply within a day, in plain language, tells you a great deal about how they will treat you afterwards.

What would you want from aftercare? Tell me.

items.hook: A patient taught me to slow my speech down
items.script:
She told me, in the kindest way, that I explained things too quickly and she felt lost. I laughed, thanked her and changed.

Now I pause, check she has understood and invite her to repeat things back. It turned out to help every patient, and my consultations improved.

Feedback is a gift, and I welcome it.

She also suggested I place a small clock on the wall behind her chair so I stay aware of my pace. It sounds simple, and it improved my consultations immediately. Now I smile when patients tell me to slow down, because it means they feel comfortable enough to say so.

Have you ever helped a professional improve? Tell me about it.

items.hook: What to do if a clinic pushes a package you did not ask for
items.script:
Pause, smile and say you would like to think about it. A genuine recommendation will still make sense tomorrow.

Ask for the plan in writing, ask what each part is for and ask what happens if you start with less. Take time to compare.

Your decision should always be yours, and a good clinic respects that.

A friendly clinic will not mind. You can also ask for a recommendation and a reason, then take a few days to compare. Be wary of free extras that come with a commitment. Calm, curious questions are your best protection, and your choice is always allowed to be nothing at all.

Has this happened to you? Tell me what you did.

items.hook: Why I keep my prices clear and my menu honest
items.script:
You see the price before you decide, and I explain what is included. If anything changes, I tell you before I begin.

Hidden extras and vague quotes create awkward moments, and I try to avoid them. A clear price gives you confidence.

Honest pricing is part of honest care.

I send you a written estimate after your consultation so you can compare it with others. If the plan changes, I explain why and update the figure. Patients tell me this transparency helps them relax, because they know exactly what they are agreeing to and what each step costs.

What do you wish clinics explained about prices? Tell me.

items.hook: How I work with a prescriber to keep treatments safe
items.script:
Some treatments require a prescription from a qualified prescriber who has assessed the patient. I work within those rules.

That means your consultation is thorough, your records are shared appropriately and a suitably qualified person signs off the plan. It adds a step and it protects you.

Ask any practitioner who prescribes, and how they work together.

Rules about prescribing exist to protect patients, and I respect them fully. If I ever feel a treatment is unsuitable, I raise it with the prescriber, and we decide together. Working as a team gives you an extra layer of oversight, and that is a good thing.

Does that make sense? Tell me what you would like me to explain more.

items.hook: Why I decline to treat when I am unwell or distracted
items.script:
My hands and mind need to be steady. If I am poorly or something has unsettled me, I rebook your appointment and apologise.

It inconveniences us both for a short while, and it keeps you safe. Patients have always been understanding.

A professional knows their limits on a given day.

I keep slots free in my diary for exactly this reason, so rescheduling is quick. I also tell you promptly and offer a priority booking next time. Honesty about my own state is part of safe practice, and patients tend to respect it deeply.

If I ever have to move you, I offer the first available appointment and a small gesture of thanks, like a hand written note. Patients tell me they would always rather hear the truth early than meet a tired practitioner on the day.

Would you rather wait a few days? Tell me.

items.hook: What the difference is between a review and a top up
items.script:
A review is a check in, where we look at how things have settled and talk about how you feel. A top up is an additional treatment you choose after the review.

I keep them separate, so you never feel you must add something to attend a review. The review comes first, and decisions follow.

You choose each step.

Reviews are free, and they are part of the service. A top up is entirely your choice, and I never pressure anyone to add one. If you feel fine after a review, we simply say goodbye until the next time. Clarity keeps the relationship pleasant and honest.

Would you like a review booked with your treatment? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I ask patients to tell me when something feels wrong
items.script:
Your instincts are valuable. If something feels odd during or after a treatment, tell me immediately.

I would far rather hear about a small worry than miss a real one. I respond calmly, check carefully and keep you informed.

You never bother me by asking.

I might ask, does that feel okay? How is your comfort? Is there anything I should know? Those questions invite honest answers. Your body gives me information, and so do your words. Together, we steer the appointment safely, and you remain in charge from start to finish.

Do you find it hard to speak up? Tell me what would help.

items.hook: How I choose which treatments to offer in my clinic
items.script:
I offer treatments that I have trained in properly, that have good evidence and that I would be comfortable recommending to my family.

I say no to trends that lack evidence or safety, even when they are popular. I keep the menu focused so I can deliver high quality care.

A shorter menu often reflects careful standards.

I also speak with colleagues and read research before adding anything new. Every addition needs training, equipment, insurance and a plan for complications. A focused menu lets me do fewer things very well. Patients tell me they appreciate a practitioner who is honest about what they offer.

Is there a treatment you wonder about? Tell me, and I will say what I think.

items.hook: Why I celebrate patients who decide against treatment
items.script:
Choosing not to proceed is a valid decision, and I respect it fully. It might mean the plan was not right, the timing was off or the idea changed.

I thank them for coming and invite them back whenever they wish. Some return in years, some never do, and I am glad either way.

A good conversation is worth having whatever the outcome.

Sometimes patients thank me for a consultation that ended without a booking, and I take that as a compliment. Good care includes protecting people from decisions they are not ready for. I also keep a friendly note in the record so future conversations feel warm and familiar.

Would you feel comfortable saying no? Tell me.

items.hook: What to bring to a follow up appointment
items.script:
Bring your questions, any photos you took, notes about how you felt and a list of any new medicines or products.

Tell me about reactions, however small. Mention events or changes in your routine. Bring your aftercare sheet if you still have it.

It helps me see the whole picture and respond properly.

A list of what you ate, drank or applied before your appointment can help too, along with any changes in medication or health. If you took photos at home, bring them. It all helps me review your progress fairly and plan the next step with confidence.

What would you like to ask at your follow up? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I treat every patient like a guest in my home
items.script:
I greet you, offer a drink, ask about your day and show you where everything is. I explain each step and check you are comfortable.

Hospitality is part of care. A relaxed patient communicates better and feels safer.

I want you to leave feeling cared for, whatever we decided.

I greet you by name, remember your dog's name or your daughter's exam and ask how things went. These small touches take little effort and mean a lot. A treatment room is also a place of trust, and warmth is part of how I earn it, every single visit.

What makes you feel welcome? Tell me.

items.hook: The standard I hold myself to, in one sentence
items.script:
I treat every patient the way I would want my mum treated.

That means honesty about options, careful safety checks, generous time, clear pricing, thoughtful aftercare and a willingness to say no.

It sounds simple, and it keeps me grounded on busy days.

It also means I turn work away sometimes, and I accept the cost. If a treatment would not suit you, I say so. If you need more time, I wait. If something goes wrong, I own it and put it right. That is the standard I would want for my own family, and I hold myself to it.

What standard would you want from someone treating your face? Tell me.

title: My Story
description: Forty nine scripts that let patients meet the person behind the chair. Adapt each anecdote so it is true for you.

items.hook: Why I chose aesthetics after years in a different career
items.script:
I spent years in a role I respected, and something kept tugging at me. I loved the moments when a patient left feeling more like themselves. Those moments stayed with me long after the shift ended.

So I trained, studied and practised until I felt ready to do it properly. It took patience, a lot of early mornings and some wobbly first days.

Looking back, I would do it all again. The best part of my week is still the moment a nervous person relaxes in my chair.

Before I started, I volunteered, shadowed colleagues and talked with practitioners about the realities of the work. I asked every difficult question I could think of. The more I learned, the surer I felt. I still keep my old notebook from that time, and I flick through it when I need reminding of my reasons.

What would you do if you could start a new chapter? Tell me in the comments, I would love to know.

items.hook: The first patient who made me cry, in a good way
items.script:
She came in nervous and quiet, and she told me she had avoided mirrors for months. We took our time, and we talked about what she wanted and what she was ready for.

At her review, she walked in smiling, shoulders down, hair done. She said she had gone to a family party and enjoyed it. I had to blink hard.

That day I understood what this work gives people. It can return a little ease to a hard season.

I remember driving home that night with a lump in my throat and a silly grin. I told my family I had helped someone feel brave. It reminded me that behind every appointment is a story, and that kindness and skill together can make a real difference to someone's week.

Has a small moment ever changed your week? Tell me about it.

items.hook: What my own first treatment felt like from the chair
items.script:
I booked my first appointment with sweaty palms. My practitioner talked me through everything and let me ask a thousand questions.

I remember noticing how much a calm voice helped. I also noticed how strange it felt to be the patient after years of being the professional.

That experience shaped how I treat people today. I explain, pause and check in often, because I remember how it feels.

That experience changed my vocabulary too. I stopped saying just a quick injection or only a small thing, because nothing feels small when it is your face. Now I acknowledge the importance of each appointment, and I treat every patient's nerves with the respect they deserve.

Have you been the nervous one in the chair? Tell me what helped you.

items.hook: A mistake from my early days that made me a better practitioner
items.script:
Early on, I rushed a consultation because I was keen to impress. A patient left unsure, and she called me a few days later with questions I should have answered in the room.

I felt dreadful. I apologised, we talked it through, and I changed my process the same afternoon. I slowed down, added a written summary and started checking understanding.

That call taught me more than any course. It shaped my approach and I still think of it.

Since then, I send a short written summary after every consultation, and I phone anyone who seems uncertain. It takes a few extra minutes, and it has prevented countless misunderstandings. I am grateful to that patient for being honest with me, because her call shaped the way I work every day.

What lesson did a mistake teach you? Tell me.

items.hook: What a typical Tuesday in my clinic looks like
items.script:
I arrive early, set up the room and read through the day's notes. Patients come in for consultations, treatments and reviews, and between them I tidy, restock and drink far too much tea.

Lunch is usually something I eat standing up. I answer messages in the afternoon, plan the next day and send aftercare check ins.

The routine sounds ordinary, and it holds many small kindnesses. I enjoy every part.

Some days there is laughter, some days tears, and some days a quiet hour with a crossword. I keep a small notebook of ideas for the next appointment. When the last patient leaves, I clean down, write my notes and walk home slowly. It is an ordinary routine that feels like a privilege.

What does your Tuesday look like? Tell me.

items.hook: Why my clinic is decorated the way it is
items.script:
I wanted it to feel like a calm friend's living room with clinical standards underneath. Soft lighting, warm colours, a comfy chair and a plant that has survived despite me.

Every item has a reason. The blanket is for chilly hands. The mirror is positioned so you see yourself in kind light. The tissues are within reach.

I think the room tells you how I work before I say a word.

I painted one wall myself, badly, and I have grown fond of it. Patients sometimes ask about the cushion, the print or the candle. These small things make the room feel like mine, and they give us something to chat about while you settle in. A warm room helps a person breathe out.

What makes a space feel welcoming to you? Tell me.

items.hook: The compliment I treasure most from a patient
items.script:
She said, you made me feel like I was the only person in the world, and I did not feel judged.

I wrote it down. I keep it in my diary and read it on difficult days. It reminds me what matters most.

Technique matters, and so does making someone feel safe. The two go together.

I think about it when I feel rushed. The best treatment in the world cannot replace the experience of being treated as a person. That compliment keeps my priorities straight, and I try to earn it every time someone sits in my chair.

What is the nicest thing someone has said to you? Tell me.

items.hook: What I do on days when I feel nervous too
items.script:
Nerves visit me too, especially before a new treatment or a big day. I breathe, check my notes and remind myself of my training.

Then I smile at the patient and let their calm guide mine. It helps that I prepare carefully and keep my routines.

Admitting it makes me more human. Nerves show I care.

My routine includes arriving early, laying out my tools and taking five slow breaths before the first patient. I also remind myself that my calm becomes your calm. Admitting nerves to myself is the first step to steadiness, and it makes me kinder to nervous patients.

How do you steady yourself before something important? Tell me.

items.hook: What I tell my sister when she asks about treatments
items.script:
She asks me everything, and I answer as honestly as I can. I tell her to take her time, to ask questions and to choose a practitioner she trusts.

I tell her that no change needs to happen, and that her face is lovely. If she decides to explore, I tell her what to look for.

It keeps me grounded to answer as a family member would.

I also tell her to be wary of anyone who rushes her, to write down her questions and to wait a week before deciding. If she ever asks me to treat her, I will say yes only if she is certain, and I will keep my promise about taking things slowly.

Who do you ask for advice? Tell me.

items.hook: How becoming a parent changed how I treat patients
items.script:
I became more patient and more attentive. I listen to the worry behind the request and I notice how people care for themselves last.

Many of my patients are parents too, and they often put themselves at the end of the list. I try to make their appointment feel like a pause.

Parenthood taught me kindness, and I bring it into the room.

I think about bedtime stories, packed lunches and the endless planning that goes into family life. My patients carry all of that too, and they often arrive tired. I make their appointment a pocket of care, and I remind them they deserve to look after themselves.

What has changed the way you work? Tell me.

items.hook: The training day that humbled me
items.script:
On a course, I watched an expert pause midway through a treatment to ask the patient a question. It made me realise how much I had still to learn about communication.

I took notes furiously and asked for feedback on my own work. I returned home with a new habit of checking in often.

Humility keeps skills sharp. I hope I never lose it.

I went home and rewrote my consultation template, adding more time for questions and a space to note how a patient feels at each stage. I felt both embarrassed and grateful. Good teachers show us what we cannot yet see, and I still thank that trainer in my head.

What humbled you recently? Tell me.

items.hook: What I wish I knew before starting my clinic
items.script:
I wish I had known how much of the job is conversation. I trained for the technical side and discovered that listening occupies most of my day.

I also wish I had trusted myself sooner. Imposter feelings visit most new practitioners, and they fade with practice and kind patients.

I wish I had asked more questions and compared fewer notes.

I also wish I had known how lonely the early months can feel. Finding a community of practitioners helped enormously. We share questions, celebrate wins and gently challenge each other. If you are thinking of starting out, find your people early.

What advice would you give your younger self? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I kept the first thank you card I ever received
items.script:
It was handwritten, a bit wobbly and full of kindness. She thanked me for listening, and for helping her feel brave.

It sits in a drawer near my desk, and I read it when I need a boost. It reminds me that we are working with people in tender moments.

Some of the best rewards cannot be measured.

I have kept every card since, tucked into a box with ticket stubs and old photos. Looking through it on a quiet evening feels like visiting a gallery of small kindnesses. They remind me that the work reaches further than I can see.

Do you keep a note that means a lot? Tell me.

items.hook: The skincare habit I never skip, whatever the day
items.script:
Sun protection, every morning. I put it on before breakfast, even in winter.

It takes ten seconds and it protects my skin for the long run. I have watched patients benefit from the same habit.

I do plenty of other things, and this is the one I recommend most.

I apply it before I leave the house, and I carry a small tube in my bag for top ups. I have tried many routines, and this simple habit has survived every one of them. If you are building a routine, start with this and add other things slowly.

What is your one habit you never skip? Tell me.

items.hook: What I do to switch off after a busy clinic day
items.script:
I take a walk, listen to music and cook something simple. I keep my phone away for an hour and let my mind settle.

Looking after myself makes me a better practitioner. A tired, frazzled version of me serves no one.

Rest is part of my professional toolkit.

I also try to read a book that has nothing to do with work. Evenings in the garden, a bath and a long phone call with a friend all help. When I feel rested, my patients feel it too, and my decisions are clearer. Looking after myself is part of looking after you.

How do you wind down? Tell me.

items.hook: A patient who changed my mind about something I believed
items.script:
I assumed a particular concern was minor, and she showed me how deeply it affected her confidence. She spoke about avoiding photos and meetings, and I realised I had underestimated it.

I thanked her and changed how I ask about concerns. Now I ask how something feels as well as how it looks.

Patients teach me constantly.

It reminded me never to guess how a worry feels from the outside. Now I ask open questions, I listen carefully and I let people describe their experiences without hurrying them along. Humility improves care, and I am thankful for the lesson.

When did someone change your mind? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I started saying "what would you like to keep?"
items.script:
I used to ask what people wanted to change. One day I added, and what would you like to keep? The answers transformed my consultations.

People named their laugh lines, their freckles, the shape of their nose. It reminded us both of what we love about a face.

Now it is a core question in my practice.

It also helps me avoid chasing perfection. When someone names their favourite feature, I can protect it. Feeling affection for your own face is a strong foundation for any plan, and I would like every patient to leave with at least one thing they love.

What do you love about your face? Tell me.

items.hook: The day a patient brought me tea and cake
items.script:
She arrived for her review with a flask and two slices of lemon drizzle. We sat and chatted before we looked at anything.

It was a lovely reminder that relationships matter in this work. Patients become friends, and the room becomes a place to share news.

I felt grateful, and I ate the cake.

We looked at her face in the afternoon light, and she told me stories about her garden. It was such a gentle visit that I almost forgot it was a work appointment. Those afternoons remind me why I chose a small clinic and a long schedule.

Who has made your day with a small gesture? Tell me.

items.hook: What I learned from a patient in her eighties
items.script:
She told me she wanted to feel fresh for her granddaughter's wedding. We talked about her skin, her health and her expectations, and she asked sensible questions.

She taught me that confidence belongs to every decade. She also taught me that grace includes knowing what you want.

I think of her often.

Her wedding photos turned out beautifully, and she sent me one with a note that made me smile. She had asked thoughtful questions, listened carefully and decided at her own pace. Working with her was a pleasure, and I learned a great deal.

We talked for a long while about the fashion of her youth, her wedding day and the joy of watching grandchildren grow. Those stories gave me a fuller picture of her than any assessment could have done.

Who taught you something about ageing well? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I get nervous before every new patient's first visit
items.script:
I hope I will be kind, thorough and useful. I want them to feel welcome from the doorway.

A flutter of nerves reminds me to prepare. I read their form, tidy the room and breathe before they arrive.

Once we start talking, the nerves melt.

Over time, I have learnt that welcome starts before the appointment. A friendly message, clear directions and a smile at the door set the tone. I want you to feel expected, and that takes a little preparation on my side.

I remember one patient who arrived ten minutes early and sat very still. I offered her a drink and a seat by the window, and we simply talked about the weather until her shoulders dropped. Starting slowly is a skill I practise every day.

What do you do before meeting someone new? Tell me.

items.hook: A moment on a treatment day that I will never forget
items.script:
A patient squeezed my hand and told me she had been dreading this for years. By the end, she was laughing at herself for worrying.

I remember the moment she exhaled. It reminded me that bravery shows up quietly.

Moments like that make the work meaningful.

Afterwards we sat and had tea, and she told me about her family. I realised how much trust she had given me. I thanked her, and I have never forgotten that hand on mine. It reminded me how important gentleness is in every step.

Later she sent me a short message to say she had thought about that moment all week. It surprised me how much a tiny gesture mattered. Since then I tell every patient that I am right here, whatever they need, throughout the appointment.

When did you do something brave? Tell me.

items.hook: The advice my mentor gave me that I still use
items.script:
Slow down. She said it kindly, again and again, until it sank in.

She taught me that a calm pace builds trust. I now pause before I begin, speak clearly and leave space for questions.

It is simple advice that has changed my practice.

She also taught me to leave a pause after I ask a question. Patients often fill the silence with the thing they most want to say. That small gap has led to some of the most honest and valuable conversations in my career.

I have repeated that advice to colleagues and trainees ever since. They often smile and say they have been going too fast as well. A slower rhythm helps me notice details, and it helps patients feel they are the only person on my diary.

What advice has stayed with you? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I still love this job after all these years
items.script:
Every patient brings a different story. I get to listen, to help and to see the relief in someone's shoulders when they feel heard.

The work blends science, art and conversation. It keeps me curious.

Some days are tiring, and I still love it.

No two days are the same, and no two faces are either. I enjoy the puzzle of listening carefully and finding the right plan for each person. That variety keeps me interested and it makes the work feel fresh.

On quiet afternoons I sometimes think back over the people I have met. Their stories fill my memory like a patchwork quilt. That sense of connection is the best part of the job, and it makes the long hours worthwhile.

What do you love about your job? Tell me.

items.hook: What my family thinks about my work
items.script:
They are proud and a little baffled. My mum tells everyone I look after people's confidence, and my partner says I come home glowing after good days.

They also tease me about the smell of antiseptic and the number of mirrors in my house.

Support at home keeps me going.

My family also help me stay grounded when I take work too seriously. They remind me to switch off, take holidays and enjoy ordinary evenings. Their support makes the long days easier, and I try to thank them often.

They tease me about the smell of antiseptic on my coat, and we laugh every time. Their teasing keeps me humble, and their pride reminds me why I started. Family is the quiet engine behind every working week.

Who cheers you on? Tell me.

items.hook: The self care I recommend to every patient
items.script:
Drink water, protect your skin from the sun, sleep when you can and laugh with people you love.

I say it often, and I mean it. Small habits shape how we look and feel.

Treatments are one option, and daily care forms the foundation.

I also remind them that sleep, laughter and time outdoors do wonders. If a treatment is helpful, brilliant. If a walk and a good night's sleep do the job, even better. I like patients to feel well in themselves from every angle.

I also tell them to be kind about their reflections. A harsh inner voice affects confidence far more than any line on a face. Speaking to yourself as you would to a friend is a free habit with real benefits.

What is your favourite way to look after yourself? Tell me.

items.hook: The question that made me rethink my whole consultation
items.script:
A patient once asked me, what do you see when you look at me? Her voice wobbled a little, and I realised she was braced for a list of flaws.

I told her what I genuinely saw: warmth in her eyes, a lovely smile and a face that had clearly laughed a lot. Her shoulders dropped. We then talked about what bothered her, from a much kinder starting point.

Now I begin every consultation by naming something I like about a person's face. It changes the whole tone of the conversation.

Since then, I have noticed how the mood changes when a patient hears something kind first. The shoulders drop, the jaw softens and the real conversation begins. It takes five seconds, and it makes every consultation warmer and more useful for both of us.

Would that feel different for you? Tell me what a good first question would be.

items.hook: The day I almost quit, and what kept me going
items.script:
Eighteen months in, I had a week where everything felt heavy. A long run of late nights, a tricky complaint and a voice in my head telling me I was not cut out for it.

A patient sent me a message that week, thanking me for the way I had listened. It arrived at the exact moment I needed it. I sat down, took a breath and decided to stay.

Looking back, that week taught me to ask for support and to remember why I started.

I took a long weekend, spoke with my mentor and rearranged my diary so I had breathing space. Small changes, such as a proper lunch break and an earlier finish, made a big difference. Asking for help was the best decision I made that year.

When did a kind word arrive at just the right time for you? Tell me.

items.hook: What my favourite patient taught me about ageing
items.script:
She is in her seventies, sharp as a tack, and she visits me once a year. She says she wants to look like herself on a lovely day, with no desire to look thirty.

She laughs easily and wears her laugh lines like medals. When we talk about her face, she mentions the stories behind each line.

She taught me that the aim is to feel at home in your own reflection, whatever your age.

She also reminds me that every face has a history. Looking at a patient, I try to see the whole life that shaped it, beyond the features. That perspective makes me gentler, more patient and more grateful for the people who sit with me.

Who showed you a gracious way of growing older? Tell me about them.

items.hook: A funny thing that happens in my treatment room every week
items.script:
Patients apologise for their faces. They say sorry for their skin, their lines, their questions and their nerves.

I tell them they never need to say sorry in my room, and it usually makes them laugh. Some say they will try to stop and then apologise for apologising.

It has become a little ritual, and I love it. The room is a place to be exactly as you are.

Last week someone apologised for her pores, her eyebrows and the temperature of her hands, all in the first two minutes. I answered with a smile and a cup of tea. By the end she had stopped apologising, and I think that was the best result of the day.

What do you find yourself apologising for? Tell me, and let us leave it at the door.

items.hook: What I carry in my bag to every appointment
items.script:
Tissues, a spare pen, a snack and a small notebook for questions. I keep a calming hand cream too, because patients often arrive with cold hands.

My notebook holds my promises, such as follow ups I owe and questions I need to research. I like to keep my word.

The contents of my bag reflect my philosophy: be prepared, be kind and be ready to listen.

I keep a spare charger, a clean scarf and a few boiled sweets for anyone who feels wobbly. These small things have rescued many a long day. A prepared practitioner has more room to give patients her full attention, which is my favourite way to work.

What is in your bag that helps you through a busy day? Tell me.

items.hook: The moment I realised honesty builds a better practice
items.script:
A patient asked me for something I felt would not suit her. I explained my view and offered an alternative. She left without booking, and I felt a pang about the lost appointment.

Three months later she returned with two friends and a long list of questions. She said she trusted me because I had been straight with her.

Honesty took longer to pay off, and it built something lasting.

It taught me that trust builds slowly and lasts a long time. I now see every conversation, booked or not, as an investment in a relationship. I try to leave people feeling respected, because respect is remembered long after the details fade.

Have you ever trusted someone because they were honest? Tell me.

items.hook: The small ritual that starts every one of my workdays
items.script:
Before the first patient arrives, I walk through the clinic with a cup of tea. I touch the back of the treatment chair, check the lighting and say a quiet good morning to the room.

It sounds silly, and it settles me. I remind myself that today someone will trust me with something personal, and that I want to be worthy of it.

Then I open the door and welcome whoever arrives.

It takes about two minutes and it changes the pace of my whole morning. Patients benefit from a practitioner who starts the day grounded. If you have a small ritual of your own, I think it is worth protecting.

Do you have a morning ritual? Tell me about it.

items.hook: What I say to patients who are nervous about telling me their worries
items.script:
I tell them that nothing they say will surprise me. I have heard worries about noses, necks, hands, scars, eyelids and everything between.

I explain that naming a worry is the first step towards understanding it. I listen, nod and ask questions. I never rush them.

Many say they felt lighter simply for saying it out loud.

I also remind them that I keep everything confidential. Some worries feel tender, and they need a safe place to be said. When a patient trusts me with them, I treat that trust as a responsibility. I listen, and I take my time with my answers.

What worry would you like to say out loud? Tell me, and I will listen.

items.hook: How I learned to trust my instincts in the treatment room
items.script:
In my early years, I second guessed every decision. Over time I noticed that my gut often noticed things before my brain caught up. A change in a patient's breathing, a hesitation or a tight jaw.

I learned to honour those signals and to pause. I check in, ask a question and adjust.

Instinct grows with experience, and I rely on it alongside my training.

I also trust my instincts about when to stop. If something feels off, I pause, reassess and ask for a second opinion where needed. Experience has taught me that caution is a strength. Patients are safer when I listen to that quiet voice.

When did you last follow your gut and feel glad? Tell me.

items.hook: What a patient's laughter in my chair means to me
items.script:
It tells me she feels safe. When someone laughs in the middle of a treatment, her face softens and her shoulders drop.

I do not aim to be a comedian, though I love a giggle. Laughter signals trust, and I treasure it.

I once made a patient laugh so hard that we had to pause for a moment. We both agreed it was worth it.

Sometimes the funniest moments come from a patient telling a story about her family. I try to keep my hands steady while smiling at the punchline. Laughter in a treatment room shows that we have built something comfortable together, and it makes my day.

What makes you laugh out loud? Tell me.

items.hook: The journal I keep about my patients' kindest words
items.script:
I keep a small notebook in my desk. When a patient says something kind, I jot it down with the date, with no names.

On a hard day, I flip through the pages. They remind me why I do this and who I serve.

Some entries are funny, some tender, and all of them keep me going.

Some entries are from people I treated years ago, and some are from this week. Reading them is like opening a window. It reminds me that small kindnesses ripple outward, and that the way I treat one person can shape their day.

Do you write down kind words? Tell me what you would add to your own list.

items.hook: Why I never schedule a treatment on my own bad days
items.script:
I learned the hard way that my mood shows in my hands. On a rotten day, I rebook, tidy my desk and go for a walk.

A steady, kind practitioner is worth waiting for, and patients appreciate honesty about it. I would rather move an appointment than offer less than my best.

I protect my diary so I can protect your experience.

It also taught me to look after my own wellbeing. I take proper breaks, I say no to extra bookings when I am tired and I protect my days off. A rested practitioner is a safer one, and that matters to every person who sits in my chair.

Do you schedule around your energy? Tell me how you manage.

items.hook: What I learned from my first complaint
items.script:
It stung. I read the message three times, made a tea and sat quietly. Then I replied kindly, asked to speak and listened.

The conversation changed my practice. I added written summaries, clearer aftercare and a follow up call. The patient and I parted on good terms.

Complaints, handled well, make a practice better.

Since then I have written a short, warm complaints policy and made sure every patient knows how to reach me. I thank people for honest feedback, because it helps me grow. A good response can turn a difficult moment into a stronger relationship.

How do you respond to feedback that hurts? Tell me.

items.hook: How I choose the music in my treatment room
items.script:
I keep it gentle, with soft instrumentals or quiet acoustic songs at a low volume. I ask each patient if they would like something else.

Music helps nerves settle, and it fills pauses without forcing conversation. Some people love a favourite playlist, so I let them choose.

Little details like this show I am thinking about your comfort.

I also carry an ordinary playlist for people who prefer a bit of normality. Sometimes a patient hums along, and her shoulders drop. Music is a gentle way to say that we are in no rush and that the room is a safe place.

What would be on your playlist? Tell me, and I will add it.

items.hook: The most unexpected thing a patient has ever asked me
items.script:
She asked whether I thought she was a good person. We had been chatting about her worries, and she wanted reassurance.

I told her kindly that I saw a thoughtful, generous woman. She cried a little, and we shared a tissue and a laugh.

The treatment room sometimes becomes a place for big questions.

I answered honestly and kindly, and I have thought about that conversation many times. It reminded me that my role includes listening to feelings that sit beneath the request. A treatment room can be an unexpected place for tenderness.

We then spoke about kindness, self worth and where it comes from. I did not give advice, since she mostly wanted company. Sometimes the best thing a practitioner can offer is a few minutes of quiet attention and a warm smile.

What question do you wish someone would ask you? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I love the quiet of an early morning clinic
items.script:
Before patients arrive, the building is still. Sunlight crosses the floor, the kettle clicks and I sort my notes.

That quiet helps me prepare mentally. I review my plan for the day and think about each person I will meet.

It gives my day a kind start.

I enjoy a cup of tea and a few minutes of silence. The stillness helps me focus on the patients I will meet that day. I notice small things, like the way the light falls, and I arrive at the first appointment feeling calm and ready.

On early mornings I like to water the plants, stretch my back and read through my notes with a cup of tea. By the time the first patient arrives, I feel settled and curious. That calm shapes how I welcome you.

When do you feel most calm? Tell me.

items.hook: What I tell myself when a result is not perfect
items.script:
I remind myself that I am human, and that a thoughtful review often resolves worries. I take notes, listen to the patient and plan a calm next step.

I acknowledge, adjust and learn.

Patience from both sides leads to good outcomes.

Patients forgive imperfection more readily than I forgive myself. They value honesty and a sincere effort to put things right. I try to match that generosity in how I treat myself, because a gentle approach helps everyone move forward.

When I feel a pang of worry, I speak to a colleague I trust. We talk it through, and I come away with a clearer plan. Support from other practitioners keeps me honest and keeps my patients safe.

How do you handle imperfect moments? Tell me.

items.hook: The friend who inspired me to take up this work
items.script:
A close friend once confided how self conscious she felt in photos. We sat in her kitchen while she described it, and I realised how much a thoughtful professional could help.

It stirred something in me. I began researching, then studying, then practising.

She is still my first call when I need an honest opinion.

Her honesty that day stayed with me. I realised that confidence is personal, and that a good practitioner can make a real difference through patience and care. I still think of that kitchen conversation when I feel unsure about the work.

She still sends me photos of her dog in funny hats, and we meet for coffee whenever our diaries allow. Having a friend like that keeps my feet on the ground and my heart in the right place.

Who inspires your work? Tell me about them.

items.hook: Why I keep a plant in every treatment room
items.script:
They make the room feel alive. Patients often comment on them, and it starts a chat.

Caring for plants teaches me patience. They grow slowly and respond to attention.

It is a small, living reminder of how I want to care for people.

Patients sometimes bring me cuttings, and I have started a little collection. It is a joyful reminder that care grows when it is looked after. The room feels warmer with something green in it, and I like that the plants have personalities.

Every spring I repot the largest one and give a cutting to a patient who admires it. It has become a little tradition. Looking after something green helps me remember to look after myself, too.

What plant lives in your home? Tell me.

items.hook: The conversation that convinced me to specialise
items.script:
A patient described a specific concern, and I realised I wanted to learn more. I signed up for further training and spent months studying.

Specialising meant saying no to some things and focusing on what I do best.

I never regretted it.

Since then, I have kept learning and refining my skills in that area, and I have grown more confident in advising patients. Focus helps me deliver better care, and it makes referrals to colleagues easier when someone needs something outside my expertise.

I found the extra training demanding and rewarding in equal measure. My notebooks filled up, my confidence grew and my patients noticed the difference. Choosing a focus helped me become better at the things that matter to you.

What have you chosen to focus on? Tell me.

items.hook: How I celebrate the small wins in my clinic
items.script:
When a nervous patient relaxes, I smile. When a review goes well, I note it. When a team member does something kind, I thank them.

Celebrating small wins keeps morale high and reminds us what matters.

We often finish the day with a biscuit.

Sometimes a patient brings a tiny gift, like a jar of honey or a handmade card, and we all feel a little richer. Those moments remind us that the work matters. I think it helps to pause and appreciate them.

Last month, we celebrated a patient who finally booked her first consultation after two years of thinking about it. It was a small step, and we marked it with a lemon biscuit and a cheerful cup of tea.

What small win did you enjoy this week? Tell me.

items.hook: What I would say to someone thinking about training in aesthetics
items.script:
Do it carefully. Choose a reputable course, ask about supervision and learn the basics of safety before the glamour.

Expect to study for a long time and to feel nervous at first. Find a mentor and ask lots of questions.

It is a rewarding path, and the best practitioners keep learning.

Learn about anatomy, safety, consent and complication management before you try to learn the latest trend. Ask whether you will have supervised practice and ongoing support. Choose teachers who are honest about the limits of their experience.

Spend time shadowing an experienced practitioner before committing. Ask what a normal week really looks like, how they handle complications and what they wish they had known. Honest answers protect you and the patients you will one day treat.

Are you considering a career change? Tell me.

items.hook: The moment I realised I'd found my voice with patients
items.script:
It happened during a consultation. I stopped reciting a script and started talking like myself. The patient relaxed, and we had a lovely, honest conversation.

I realised that authenticity was my strength. Patients responded to real warmth, and I felt more confident.

From then on, I trusted my own voice.

After that, I felt less like an actor playing a role and more like a person caring for another person. My consultations became shorter, kinder and more useful. Finding your voice takes time, and patients can tell when you have found it.

I remember leaving the clinic that evening with a lighter step. Nothing about my technique had changed, and the difference was that I felt at ease being myself. Patients seem to relax when I do, and the conversations have been better since.

When did you find yours? Tell me.

items.hook: Why I want every patient to leave feeling like themselves
items.script:
Because that is the point. I want you to look in the mirror and recognise the person looking back.

Every decision I make is guided by that. I choose gently, review often and listen carefully.

The best compliment is when a friend says you look well.

Many patients tell me they would like to look like themselves, on their best day. That phrase guides me. It reminds me to protect character, keep expression and respect the person behind the face.

When a friend says you look well, or when a patient tells me she feels like herself again, I know the plan worked. That gentle response is the result I value most, and it is the one I plan every treatment around.

What would you like to feel when you leave my clinic? Tell me.

title: Behind the Chair
description: Fifty scripts for the daily life, the routines and the little extras that make a clinic feel kind.

items.hook: Aftercare in plain English: what to expect in the first week
items.script:
Straight after a treatment, you may notice redness, small bumps, tenderness or a little swelling. These tend to settle over hours or days, depending on what we did.

Keep your skin clean, avoid touching the area and skip heat, heavy exercise and alcohol for the period I suggest. Use sun protection every morning, and sleep with an extra pillow if I recommend it.

Between days three and seven, things usually look calmer, and your final result keeps developing. If anything concerns you, message me straight away. I would rather answer a small question than leave you worrying overnight.

The first twenty four hours matter most, so I send a message that evening to see how you feel. By day two, most patients tell me they have forgotten about it. If your skin feels itchy or hot, or if swelling increases, contact me promptly. Following the plan carefully helps your skin settle well.

Which part of aftercare do you find trickiest? Tell me, and I will make it simpler.

items.hook: What my treatment room looks like and why each thing is there
items.script:
A comfortable chair that reclines, so you can relax. Soft light that shows your face fairly. A mirror within reach, so you can see what I see. A tray of single use items, opened in front of you.

A sharps bin, a hand basin and a clean surface for everything. A blanket for chilly patients and a tissue box for tears or laughter. A wall of certificates, because I am proud of them and you are welcome to read them.

Every item has a job. Come and see for yourself.

The decor is simple on purpose. I want the clinical parts to feel safe and the rest to feel warm. If you spot something you would like to ask about, please do. I enjoy explaining the equipment, and I think knowing what everything does makes people feel more at ease.

What would you like to find in a treatment room? Tell me, and I will share what I think.

items.hook: Things patients say to me that make me smile
items.script:
I hear, I look awful today, at least once a day. I hear, sorry, I have not shaved my legs, which is helpfully irrelevant. I hear, can you make me look like my passport photo, and I tell them that passport photos are cruel.

Someone asked if I could fix the way her husband snores. Someone else asked for advice on her tomato plants.

My room is a place for honest, human conversation, and I love it.

A patient once told me I had the loveliest ceiling, because she had spent a lot of time looking at it. We laughed so much we had to pause. Humour is welcome in my room, as long as it keeps your comfort at the centre. A shared laugh is a lovely way to settle nerves.

What is the funniest thing you have said in a clinic? Tell me, I could use a laugh.
